item.title: Jaguars keep climbing in NFL power rankings entering Week 5
item.description: Jacksonville is the best team in the AFC, some are saying.
item.content:encoded:
The respect is finally coming.

After taking care of business in Week 4, the Jacksonville Jaguars now sit at 3-1. They have a convincing first-place lead in the division — and their chances to earn the top seed in the conference continue to rise.

“I don’t think we really care about the credit,” safety Antonio Johnson said Monday. “We’re going to go into each week, and if you don’t look at us as an imposing defense, then we’re going to impose our will on you. If you don’t respect us, then we’re going to make you respect us. I know personally, in the rooms that I’ve talked to the players, we don’t care about the respect. You don’t respect us, cool. We’re going to make you respect us, so we’re not even tripping about that.”

As Week 5 approaches, we rounded up the latest NFL power rankings to get a sense of how the Jaguars are viewed nationally.

Sports Illustrated: 2 (last week: 5)

From Conor Orr:

I had a good time at the expense of the Jaguars in the immediate aftermath of the Travis Hunter trade-up. I have since retained a crisis management firm to help aid the fallout when all of my old posts get sent to Old Takes Exposed. Just look at this dude. 

Pro Football Talk: 3 (5)

From Mike Florio:

The Jaguars have the best shot at winning the No. 1 seed in the AFC.

Yahoo Sports: 4 (7)

From Frank Schwab:

Jacksonville is second to San Francisco in DVOA, and that seems like the right spot. The Jags have blown out the Browns and Patriots, who are 5-1 against everyone else. They won at the Bengals, who had started the season 2-0 and are considered dangerous. The loss to the Broncos was unfortunate, but Jacksonville led 10-3 at halftime and it’s not the first team to fade in the second half at altitude early in the season. Had it not been for that second half at Denver, Jacksonville would have a case to be the No. 1 team in these rankings. The Jaguars are very good.

NFL.com: 5 (7)

From Nick Shook:

The Jaguars have established a clear identity through four weeks: The offense seeks to establish a credible running threat and then works off the efforts of Trevor Lawrence, allowing the defense — a unit that is better than its reputation suggests — to do its job by earning an extra possession or two for Lawrence and Co. In Week 4, that strategy saw Jacksonville build a 10-point lead by halftime and secure a big road win over a talented Bengals team. The Jags’ 13 penalties prevented them from enjoying an easier second half, though. That’s something they’ll need to clean up.

CBS Sports: 5 (7)

From Pete Prisco:

They are a complete team on both sides of the ball. They can win with offense, but the defense is sneaky good and is second in scoring.

Bleacher Report: 5 (8)

From Brent Sobleski:

Jacksonville has allowed the NFL’s second-fewest points (53) through four games. The effort is also the franchise’s best since the start of the 2007 campaign. The Jaguars are particularly good at the point of attack. They’re ranked second in rushing defense after the Cincinnati Bengals managed a measly 23 yards during Sunday’s action.

ESPN: 5 (10)

From Michael DiRocco:

Four words to describe the first four weeks: Defense is getting overlooked. Heading into this season, there was plenty of hype around Year 2 of the Liam Coen offense. But defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile has made a name for himself early in the season, which could lead to attention in next year’s head-coaching cycle. The Jaguars rank among the top eight in the NFL in sacks, run defense, turnovers, red zone efficiency and third-down defense. With a run defense ranked second in the NFL (74.3 yards per game), Jacksonville has given up just nine first-half points.

USA Today: 6 (8)

From Nate Davis:

Bend but don’t break? They rank 26th overall in total defense, yet the Jags haven’t allowed more than 20 points in their past 10 regular-season games.

Fox Sports: 6 (10)

From Ralph Vacchiano:

With their win over the Bengals, the Jaguars are now 11-1 over their last 12 regular season games, the best record in the NFL in that span.

The Athletic: 6 (10)

From Josh Kendall and Chad Graff:

There’s little shame in allowing a lot of yards through the air to the Bengals. But it’s not ideal that the Jaguars allowed Joe Burrow to throw for 428 yards while Ja’Marr Chase left early due to injury. That said, Travis Hunter played only as a defensive back and looks really good there. Jacksonville appears to be trending in the right direction.

item.title: NFL Power Rankings: Giants hit Top 15 before Week 5
item.description: The Giants are quickly becoming a team to watch.
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants have quickly become a team to watch in the NFC. On paper so much should be going wrong for them with the loss of Jaxson Dart and top pass rusher Brian Burns, but instead we’ve seen John Harbaugh turn this team into a winner with some swagger, now sitting atop the NFC East and looking down on those around them.

It’s fair to note that two of their three wins have come against the Cardinals and Titans — but in the past you could never count on the Giants to close out these kinds of games, especially while battling through serious injury. We’ve yet to see this team at its best, and yet they’re still on the right side of the win column after one month in the league. They deserve their flowers, cracking the Top 15 in our Power Rankings ahead of Week 5.

Here’s our full ranking of all 32 teams, as well as their previous rank and how it changed since Week 4.

Biggest Rise: New York Giants (+10)

The Giants are passing the eye test right now too. That’s less about their football being pretty, because it often isn’t — but it’s about how the team is carrying itself on the sideline. The biggest thing Harbaugh has done for New York is improve its locker room culture to the point where these players believe they can win any game, like they’re being led by a much grumpier Ted Lasso.

Biggest Fall: Detroit Lions (-6) and Washington Commanders (-6)

This Lions defense is just so, so, so bad. Granted, they were playing Bryce Young on Sunday Night Football, who is playing out of his mind — but the Panthers were also without four offensive linemen, as well as their No. 2 and No. 3 receivers (Jalen Coker and Xavier Legette). With essentially one good receiver, the Panthers sliced and diced the Detroit secondary using the RPO, basically making a blueprint for whoever wants to attack it. It’s growing more and more difficult to see how the Lions hang with the Bears in the NFC North.

As for the Commanders, this is some course correction. We were bullish on Washington returning to form in 2026, but there’s been nothing to indicate they’re worthy of faith. Moreover, the team is getting worse as time goes on, struggling more against worse opponents — and the injury bug is creeping in. It’s a shame, but this is shaping up to be another lost season for the team.

Team to Watch: Atlanta Falcons (No. 21)

Getting the doors blown off against the Panthers in Week 2 might have been the best thing to happen to the Falcons this season. The team looks completely different following their divisional embarrassment, now boasting a really solid all-around defense despite lacking their top pass rushers, and having an offense that can lean on Bijan Robinson to carry them over the finish line. There’s so much to like about this team other than its shaky QB position, but all in all, the Falcons are looking like a team that could contend in the NFC South and make a push into the top half of the league.

item.title: Week 5 NFL Power Rankings: Where do the 49ers rank among undefeated teams?
item.description: The Niners keep moving up the power rankings after another win.
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers are only one of three NFL teams that have started the season 4-0 in 2026, joining the Kansas City Chiefs and the Minnesota Vikings. Thus far, their +58 point differential leads the NFL, and they also have two big wins on their resume: the Los Angeles Rams and the Denver Broncos.

The 49ers have had some flaws, with injuries being the biggest issue. San Francisco is well short at wide receiver and defensive line, going deeper and deeper into their practice squad pool. But they’ve been even better than advertised through four weeks, taking advantage of an early three-game home stand.

There were several teams that had impressive wins in Week 5. The Jacksonville Jaguars beat the Cincinnati Bengals. The Dallas Cowboys put up 34 points on the Houston Texans. The New England Patriots came from behind to beat the Buffalo Bills on the road. So did the Rams against the Philadelphia Eagles.

Remaining undefeated, where are the 49ers in this week’s power rankings?

ESPN: No. 1

“The 49ers have again been hit by a slew of injuries,” ESPN’s Nick Wagoner wrote. “On the defensive line, star defensive end Nick Bosa is out because of a calf issue. At receiver, they’ve lost Ricky Pearsall (knee) for the season and promising rookie De’Zhaun Stribling (ankle) for 10 weeks.

“And yet the Niners are one of three undefeated teams. Quarterback Brock Purdy has emerged as an early MVP candidate, as the offense has done most of the heavy lifting. But Sunday’s win showed the Niners can lean on their defense and special teams when they aren’t lighting up the scoreboard.”

The Chiefs, Seahawks, Bills, and Jaguars rounded out the top five.

USA Today: No. 1

“Given their largely tremendous start, would have put them in the top spot sooner if not for concern regarding their latest rash of injuries, FB Kyle Juszczyk the most recent star to go down,” USA Today’s Nate Davis wrote.

“However, the Niners are certainly safeguarding early MVP candidate Brock Purdy, becoming the first team since Peyton Manning’s 2005 Colts to permit zero sacks through four games. Beat Seattle on Sunday, and San Francisco will have already taken down three of last season’s final four teams. Unbeaten through four games for the third time under Kyle Shanahan, now the longest-tenured coach in franchise history, the 49ers leveraged those other two hot starts into Super Bowl berths.”

Here, the Chiefs, Seahawks, Broncos, and Rams closed off the top five.

CBS Sports: No. 1

“At 4-0, they are rolling, and beating good teams in the process. The defense came up big in the victory over the Broncos, which is a good sign,” CBS’s Pete Prisco wrote.

Behind them were the Chiefs, Vikings, Seahawks, and Jaguars.

Overall, most places had the 49ers initially at No. 2, bumping them to No. 1 after their win over the Broncos and Buffalo’s loss to New England.

San Francisco will get a big challenge, though, in Week 5, as they take on the Seattle Seahawks on the road. They’re currently three-point underdogs ahead of kickoff.

item.title: 7 NFL truths we already believe after 4 weeks
item.description: This is what we’re buying at the start of the NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Four weeks of play in the NFL is where the rubber starts to meet the road. Everyone has had time to ease their way into the season, with teams more or less running where they should be for the remainder of the year. It’s been one of the most surprising starts to a season in recent memory, with locks plummeting, underdogs rising, and a full shakeup coming around the league.

While it still feels very early to make bold predictions about how this season will play out, we do have some thoughts based on what we’ve seen happen in the season. Here are the things we think we know about the NFL after four weeks.

We’re going to see an unlikely MVP in 2026

It’s growing increasingly likely that we’re going to see a surprise in the MVP race this year. We had the usual suspect favorites before the season began in Josh Allen, Matthew Stafford, Lamar Jackson, and Joe Burrow — but it’s feeling like none of those guys have an edge at this point in the season.

Allen is still playing good football, but early in the season he’s taken a small step back from his 2025 form. As for the rest of the favorite field, it’s a mixed bag. Stafford has been mediocre; Jackson has been good, but the injury bug is creeping in, while Joe Burrow has been excellent, but not electric.

There is a wide-open door for some guys to make a dark horse run. Brock Purdy leads the NFL in passing touchdowns along with … Kirk Cousins?! Bryce Young is the league leader in passing right now. At running back we have Kenneth Walker and Bijan Robinson on pace for over 2,000 yards each. Then there’s CeeDee Lamb, who is trending towards a 2,000 yard receiving season with 17+ touchdowns.

Right now there is simply a ludicrous amount of talent who weren’t the preseason favorites, and the odds that they will all struggle for the remainder of the season is slim. I think we’re going to see a major shock when the end of season voting rolls around.

The Eagles are in trouble

Philadelphia is sitting at 2-2 on paper, which really isn’t that bad — but the vibes feel off with this football team. Even looking at the Eagles’ two wins, they only managed single-score victories over the Commanders and Titans, and are currently sitting at a significant scoring differential of -18. This puts them on par with the New York Jets, Pittsburgh Steelers, and Tampa Bay Buccaneers — hardly the company they want to keep.

Offensively the team is a mess, and while the defense is keeping them in games, they’ve yet to really face an elite team this season, with their combined opponents’ W/L record sitting at 6-10. Something has to change to save their season, and fast.

Patrick Mahomes and the Chiefs are back

Doubting the Chiefs is the NFL equivalent of “fool me once, shame on you — fool me twice, shame on me.” Every single time this team gets counted out they manage to rebound, and once more we’re seeing Kansas City become one of the top teams in the league.

Patrick Mahomes is quietly having a massive bounce-back, which is wild considering there’s never been much quiet around Pat Mahomes. Meanwhile, the defense has been as good as any in the NFL, allowing only 77 points across four games and ensuring the job for the offense is as easy as possible.

With a legitimate running back in Kenneth Walker, the Chiefs look like they’re poised to make another deep run in the AFC after missing the playoffs a year ago. This team is back.

The Carolina Panthers are for real

Carolina’s overall record of 2-2 hardly leaps off the page, but something special is brewing in Charlotte. Now entering their bye week, the Panthers are running one of the NFL’s best offenses despite having a patchwork offensive line riddled with injury holes, while being banged up at wide receiver. Now the Panthers are poised to get back as many as NINE players, including FIVE starters from injured reserve or short-term injury after their bye, fully reloading before they hit the midpoint of the season.

It’s too early to tell whether this is a legitimate contender (they probably aren’t due to defensive issues), but the fact is that the Panthers are not an easy out on the schedule anymore. Looking ahead at their slate every game feels winnable for them now, with eight feeling like games where they now have the edge.

So are the Las Vegas Raiders

Sunday’s loss to the Kansas City Chiefs dropped the Las Vegas Raiders from the unbeaten ranks.

But in that loss, Kirk Cousins and the Raiders showed that they are indeed back.

Through four weeks the Raiders have been perhaps the most surprising story of the NFL season, but in Sunday’s loss Las Vegas showed they could indeed play with the NFL’s best. The Raiders took a lead in the fourth quarter on a Matt Gay field goal, and just when you thought a difficult sequence ended any chance of a Las Vegas win — the Chiefs not only took a 23-19 lead on their ensuing possession but a fumble on the ensuing kickoff set the stage for a second Kansas City touchdown in a matter of seconds to give the Chiefs a 30-19 lead — the Raiders stormed back.

The late rally fell short, but the Raiders are for real.

We buried the Falcons too soon

After two weeks, the Atlanta Falcons were 0-2 thanks to one of the worst passing games in recent NFL history.

Much has changed since then.

Yes, the return of Michael Penix Jr. is a part of that. The young quarterback completed 18-of-25 passes for 256 yards, a touchdown, and an interception in a 35-14 win over the Green Bay Packers back in Week 3, and followed that up with a 15-for-20 outing against the New Orleans Saints on Monday night, throwing for 223 yards and a touchdown in a 45-24 win. The passing game, which was dismal in the hands of Cooper Rush and Jack Strand, has taken a massive step forward.

But the Falcons have also remembered they have Bijan Robinson, one of the premier talents in the game. While he was held below the 100-yard mark in each of the first two weeks, Robinson ripped off 194 yards and a pair of touchdowns against the Packers, and another 145 yards and two scores against New Orleans.

Suddenly, this team we buried after two weeks looks like a potential problem in the NFC.

Things are rotten with the Texans and Chargers

Two teams we thought were a lock for the postseason in the AFC are now both 0-4. Everything is going wrong for the Texans and Chargers, and while it’s fair to note they are both dealing with injuries, neither looks like they’ll even make it to the playoffs, let alone contend.

What’s so wild about both organizations is the surprising ways in which they’re struggling. The Texans defense has crumbled, allowing 109 points so far (26th in the NFL), while the normally safe Justin Herbert has turned into a turnover machine, with six interceptions in four games.

In both cases it feels like a freight train that’s running away from their respective coaches, and it’s unclear if either can get their teams back on track.

item.title: Whispers: Is the Cardinals’ backup QB Gardner Minshew on the trade block?
item.description: Over a month remains before the league trade deadline
item.content:encoded:
The 2026 NFL season is still young. It’s just Week 4, and anything can happen. Before the season began, the Cleveland Browns were projected to be a five-win team, while the Houston Texans had been penciled into the AFC Championship Game. Currently, the Browns are 3-1-0 while the Texans are 0-4-0.

The Arizona Cardinals are on the brink of their season. This weekend’s contest against the New York Football Giants was a pivotal game. A win would place them at .500, while a loss tosses the club into the spiraling dumpster with numerous difficult games ahead of them. Arizona was on the doorstep with a first down at the four-yard line and could not punch it in with four plays in the 36-24 loss.

RELATED: 3 SECRET SUPERSTARS ON THE 2026 ROSTER

Around the NFL, there have been a few trades already. The Dallas Cowboys just traded for safety Joey Porter Jr., while the Giants spent a fifth-round draft pick for QB J.J. McCarthy.

The NFL trade deadline is not until Tuesday, November 10 at 4:00 pm (Eastern). That means nobody is up against the final day to improve their roster, but even early in the season, coaches find weaknesses and are desperate to apply a remedy so the season doesn’t slip away.  

The Cardinals have three healthy quarterbacks. So far, Jacoby Brissett has maintained himself as a good game manager but isn’t considered an elite quarterback, and probably never will. In 2026, before the Giants game, he was ranked #17 in total passing yards (652), #6 in attempts (117), #64 in yards per attempt (5.6), and tied for sixth in touchdown passes (4) against only one interception.

Now, Brissett is ranked #20. The most glaring stat change is that his interception column went from one to four.

One thing Brissett has always been is durable. He rarely gets hurt. Over his 11-year NFL career, he has mainly been the backup signed to every roster, but has suddenly been thrust into a starting role with Arizona this year.

With Brissett at the helm, veteran Gardner Minshew is his experienced backup, and the rookie Carson Beck is on the roster. There are rumors swirling that Minshew might be traded to a team that has either lost its starting quarterback or has moved their backup into the starting role and needs a dependable backup.

NFL Insider Jason La Canfora of Casino.org has reported that Minshew is the most obvious quarterback to be available to any QB-needy roster. He stated:

“(Minshew) can give you some energy and run around and make some things happen for a few weeks until he hits the wall.  There will be turnovers, but he is game and will move the pocket and try to compete.”

The thought process is that a team, such as the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, has lost their starting QB due to injury and will need a guy to come in for a few games. Minshew fits that bill. La Canfora has stated that an NFL GM told him that Minshew will be gone by the NFL trade deadline.

“Jacoby Brissett is fully solidified as the starter, and rookie Carson Beck is still healing up from a rib injury but would make sense moving into the QB 2 role.”

Let’s examine this scenario a bit.   

For one, what would the Cardinals get in return for Minshew? Currently, he is paid $5.75 million as Arizona’s backup QB, which is cheap help. So, if Brissett were injured, the club would be paying their new starter low dough. It’s not like Minshew is getting upwards of $25 million a season to sit and wait for his opportunity. His contract is focused on him being the backup. He chose to sign with the Cardinals instead of sitting and waiting for the phone to ring, and is on an NFL roster.

What would become Minshew’s trade value? Most likely a third-day draft pick, such as a fifth-round selection and a bag of footballs.

How would this Cardinals roster change with another guy in the fifth round?

This is what will change if Arizona does move Minshew: suddenly, their backup QB is a rookie who has yet to appear in a regular-season NFL game. Minshew has played in 63 NFL games with 47 starts and has plenty of live game experience, and yes, he may never play a single game this year. But he was signed with one thing in mind: an experienced player who can come in and start if an injury happens.

This scenario occurred last year. Patrick Mahomes of the Kansas City Chiefs was hurt, and Minshew played in four games.   

Beck looked absolutely great in the Hall of Fame Game. In that game, he injured his rib and was taken off the practice list until it healed completely. He would move into Minshew’s position as QB2. Is that okay? Is that a good strategy? Basically, Beck has played in one contest – an exhibition. And that’s it. Plus, he went up against the other team’s #2 defense all game. Now, it is big-boy football going on, and Beck is not battle-tested whatsoever.

How will that 2027 fifth-round draft pick help this roster this season? Would it be prudent to insert a rookie without any NFL game experience as the starter to fill out this year’s schedule?

Plus, after the Giants loss, if Brissett continues to play that poorly, isn’t it possible that Minshew could be moved into the starting position? Isn’t that more valuable than a fifth-round draft pick.

One thing is for certain: at some point, the Cardinals will need to play Beck during a string of games to find out what they have before next year’s NFL Draft.

Another thing: the Cardinals have zero obligation to help another NFL team with their quarterback issues. So why ship off the only other experienced signalcaller for a hot dog and a bag of chips?

item.title: Steelers bring KJ Henry back to their practice squad
item.description: For the third time in the last 12 months, pass rusher KJ Henry has signed with the Steelers.
item.content:encoded:
For the third time in the last 12 months, pass rusher KJ Henry has signed with the Steelers.

Henry is signing to Pittsburgh's practice squad, according to Mike Garafolo.

The Steelers also signed Henry to their practice squad on October 11 of last year, and then after he ended last season on the Browns' practice squad, the Steelers re-signed him to a futures contract in January before cutting him in June.

Now that defensive lineman Derrick Harmon has gone on injured reserve, the Steelers need more depth in their defensive front, and so Henry is back for a third time.

Henry originally arrived in the NFL as a fifth-round pick of the Commanders out of Clemson in 2023. He has also spent time with the Bengals, Cowboys, Eagles and 49ers. He has played in 15 games in his NFL career and recorded 2.5 sacks.

item.title: Texans vs. Titans game in Week 5 is so bad that even The Weather Channel is dunking on it
item.description: No one is interested in a Week 5 battle between two winless teams.
item.content:encoded:
What happens when you pit two miserable and directionless 0-4 teams against each other in Week 5 of the NFL season? You get a game so bad even The Weather Channel is dunking on it.

The Houston Texans and the Tennessee Titans will square off in Week 5 in a game that should — barring a tie — give one of those teams their first win of the 2026 season. If you're not a fan of either team, watching the contest is a tough sell. The Titans haven't shown much improvement in Cam Ward's second season and the Texans' previously excellent defense has proven vulnerable.

Because of that, the NFL Memes account tried to shoot out an easy joke suggesting the game should be flexed to The Weather Channel, as a national audience shouldn't be subjected to the contest.

There was just one problem with that joke: Even The Weather Channel has no interest in airing Texans vs. Titans.

I’m gonna pass

— The Weather Channel (@weatherchannel) October 5, 2026

That's … pretty bleak. If The Weather Channel has no interest in broadcasting a bad NFL game, how can CBS hope to salvage the contest?

It should be obvious, but the whole thing is pretty clearly a joke. But with sporting events suddenly split between seemingly every available network and streaming service, it's worth pointing out that The Weather Channel is one of the few networks that does not own broadcast rights to NFL games. Given the state of television and streaming in 2026, though, we can't rule out a future NFL broadcast on the network.

While the Titans do seem stuck in the mud, there is some hope the Texans turn things around. The team has played some strong offenses thus far, perhaps explaining why the defense has seemingly taken a step back so far.

A possible get-right game against the Titans could get the Texans back on track. And while an 0-4 record will be tough to overcome, there is some precedent for a massive turnaround. The 1992 San Diego Chargers managed to rally from an 0-4 start to make the playoffs.

They are the only team to pull off that feat, however, so the Texans would have a lot of work to do if the team managed to win in Week 5.

item.title: Mike Washington couldn’t ignite run game in Week 4
item.description: How did Las Vegas’ rookie class fare in Week 4?
item.content:encoded:
Here is a look at how the Las Vegas Raiders’ 2026 draft class (eight of the 10 picks are on the 53-man roster) fared in a 30-27 Week 4 home loss to the Kansas City Chiefs and what to look for Sunday at the New England Patriots:

Fernando Mendoza:
The No. 1 overall pick served as Kirk Cousins backup. He hasn’t played all season.

Treydan Stukes:

The Raiders’ second-round pick returned from being out with a concussion in Week 3 and he played all 60 defensive snaps. He nearly had an interception and finished with two tackles.

Trey Zuhn:

The third-round pick played five offensive plays in a Jumbo set and he played two special teams snaps. He missed some time with an injury, but he returned.

Jermod McCoy:

The fourth-round pick played 17 snaps on special teams. He didn’t play defense for the third time in four games. He has played 18 defensive snaps this season.

Mike Washington:

The fourth-round pick played a season-high 18 snaps and he had a season-high nine carries. He finished with just 18 yards. He has 24 carries for 110 yards. He also had his first catch for minus-1 yard receiving. While he didn’t get anything going Sunday, it wouldn’t be a surprise if the Raiders use Washington more gain at New England in an attempt to spark a lacking ground game.

Dalton Johnson:

The fifth-round pick safety was active for the first time. He played 12 special-teams snaps. It will be interesting to see if he continues to be active.

Zeke Masses:

The fifth-round pick played all but two snaps against the Chiefs. He flashed as usual for the most part.

Malik Benson:

The sixth-round pick played seven offensive snaps with no targets. He had one punt return for four yards.

item.title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the New York Jets
item.description: Chicago grinded out another home win this week without their start QB. @BryanOrenchuk shares his 3 reasons the Bears earned the W.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome back to the fourth installment of my new series for the 2026 season, where I recap what I believe were the three reasons the Chicago Bears won or lost the previous game.

In week 4, the Bears hosted the feisty New York Jets and controlled the game from start to finish, dominating the time of possession and coming away with a gritty win once again without Caleb Williams as he recovers from his hamstring injury. Here are my three reasons why they won.

1. Kyle Monangai, RB

Though the 2nd year player out of Rutgers has had one game where he had more rushing yards than the 149 he racked up on the ground against the Jets, and five games where he did so with more yards per carry than the 4.9 he had, he has never scored more than once like he did and never had 30 carries before either. Considering he was clearly the best player on the field for both teams, I will henceforth be referring to this performance as the “Monangai Game” until further notice.

What impressed me most about the New Jersey native was the nature by which his success came. He was getting met at or behind the line of scrimmage early in this one and ended the first half with only 49 yards rushing. But he seemed to get stronger as the game wore on, consistently bouncing off would-be tacklers or peeling away from them for extra yardage before sporadic bursts through the line for chunk gains. You could tell he was wearing on the defense and clearly Ben Johnson could tell as well considering he saw 30 carries to D’Andre Swift’s 15. On a day where the Bears struggled to put the ball in the endzone and score TDs, Monangai seemed like the difference in this one and the main reason Chicago came away with a W. Shout out to the offensive line for continuing to pound away at the formidable Jets defensive line and the wide receivers and tight ends for committing to the gameplan as well. When you have a back like Monangai, you never know when he will break away and use your block for more yardage.

2. Rome Odunze, WR

Speaking of best games, this was easily Rome’s best game of the season as well. What stood out to me regarding Odunze’s performance, aside from marveling at how a WR his size (6’3”, 215lb) moves in and out of his breaks, was how seamlessly he caught the ball this week and the clutch nature of his catches. All game, it seemed like Rome was coming up big on 3rd down and was a large reason why we were able to move the ball down the field, especially in the first half before Monangai took over. Rome’s 94 receiving yards paced both teams in this one, and he did so on just 7 targets with 6 catches for 15.7 yards per catch and a season-best 85.7 catch percentage. Rome played with confidence and power as both a pass-catcher and run-blocker, and his presence was felt throughout this win.

3. Cairo Santos, K

On a day when the offense struggled to find the endzone, especially in the red zone, it sure was nice to have such an automatic kicker on your side. Especially in the Windy City, with gusts coming off the lake as they do. Though none of his kicks were longer than 30 yards, Santos helped keep this game out of reach for a Jets comeback. Without Santos, I am not sure Ben elects to kick the FG which made it a three score game in the 4th quarter, which could have changed the entire outcome in this one. Ben trusts him, and his teammates do too, and it showed up this week.

What about you? Who or what caught your attention against the Jets?

item.description: The fans showed up for the Saints, unfortunately the game didn't go as expected.
item.content:encoded:
In all honesty, after getting your teeth kicked in the way the Saints just did in primetime, there really isn’t a player of the game. It is worth noting that Chris Olave played great again, but that’s not worth much when the team gets embarrassed the way it just did.

The true MVPs of this game, however, were the fans.

Shoutout to the entire city of New Orleans, which was on 10 from the moment the sun came up. New Orleans was ready and excited for what this game represented: the 20-year celebration of the reopening of the Superdome after Hurricane Katrina.

The atmosphere inside the Dome at kickoff was electric. I spoke with former Saints wide receiver Lance Moore after the game, and he said the Dome felt like the Dome again. And that is exactly what it should be.

The fans were ready to roll. The excitement was there, and every single one of you, whether you were at home, at work, or at the stadium, just wanted that moment to shout, “Who Dat!”

The Saints did a great job of having Steve Gleason lead the Who Dat chant at the start of the game, with his son by his side raising his hand. The emotions were nearly overwhelming as a fan, seeing all of the pageantry that went into this game. The former players from 20 years ago were present on the sideline for kickoff. It was beautiful to see.

And then the game started.

All of that went away because, for the next three hours, the play on the field did not match the expectations and hope that Saints fans had going into the night.

Who Dat Nation, you all are this week’s Canal Street Chronicles MVP.

item.title: Tuesday Miami Dolphins Thoughts With The Earl
item.description: SO close… yet so far.
item.content:encoded:
The Dolphins hung tight with the Kansas City Chiefs for most of the game, but somehow that game never felt close.  The Dolphins not only had a chance in this game against Minnesota, but they also actually held a lead.  Well, for about 30 seconds.  Still, this one was a heartbreaking loss because unlike the previous 3 games, they felt like they could win.  There were some more positives, but plenty of negatives.  Here’s what I saw on a quick watch.

THE OFFENSIVE NEEDS… WORK

First, I will give credit where credit is due.  The Vikings have one of the best defenses in the NFL.  They generate a ton of pressure and have the best scoring defense in the NFL.  They have held better offenses to less.  The Bears scored 59 points in week one against the Panthers.  The Vikings held them to 3 points at their home.  The Vikings have only allowed 4 TDs all season, one of which was to the Dolphins.

That said, the Dolphins’ offense was nothing short of terrible on Sunday.  Willis struggled mightily, going 9-17 and 85 yards.  He was sacked twice, though one of those sacks was a “strip sack” where the ball hit a defender’s helmet right before Willis was able to throw it.  Despite the best pressure defense in the league, the Dolphins mostly kept Willis clean.  The bigger issue in my opinion is the lack of playmakers helping their QB (hat tip to JUK).  Willis targeted 6 WRs in the contest and only Malik Washington was the only one to contribute in a meaningful way.  Rookie Chris Bell was blanked on 3 targets.  Greg Dulcich wasn’t even targeted.  Without Caleb Douglas, the Dolphins don’t have the weaponry to consistently move the chains and have a productive offense.  Some of the blame will go to Willis and rightfully so.  But he doesn’t have the help he needs either.  This would be the same for a rookie this season OR next season.  Unless Miami goes out in FA and signs a big time WR or TE – unlikely – then whatever rookie QB they draft will also struggle thanks to the skill players around him.

THE DEFENSE ALSO NEEDS WORK DESPITE SOME POSITIVES

There is a lot being made about how the defense stepped up in this game.  They finally got home to the QB getting 4 sacks after getting shutout the previous 3 games.  The Dolphins were able to generate pressure all game long.  Linebackers Rodriguez and Brooks had a combined 31 tackles, with the rookie getting 18 total and 9 solo tackles.  The Dolphins kept the Vikings out of the end zone, forcing 5 FG attempts.  But…

The Vikings were an even worse offense than the Dolphins entering this game. In week one, the Vikings QBs passed for 151 yards.  In week 2, that number was 143.  In week 3, they went for 168 yards.  Against Miami, Murray went for 247 yards.  In the previous 3 contests, the Vikings barely topped 62% CP in one game and 55% or below in the other 2.  Murray went 27-37 against the Dolphins, for a whopping 72.9%.  Wildly, that’s lower than what Miami had been allowing at over 80%.  But they couldn’t contain what had been the worst passing offense in the league.  The Vikings were able to do it without Justin Jefferson also.  The damage came from tight end TJ Hockenson, whom the Dolphins could not stop.  He caught 13 passes on 13 targets for 119 yards and would have scored a TD at the end but slid to force kneel-downs and end the game.  Considering the Vikings #2 WR Jordan Addison was quietly 4-52, you would think the Dolphins would have forced Murray to look at someone other than Hockenson.  But no.  Not only that, but the Dolphins had been tighter against the run in the 1st 3 games.  But they allowed Aaron Jones to go 20 carries for 94 yards.  Murray went 6 for 16, but lost 5 yards on 3 kneel-downs, so he gained 21 yards on 3 actual attempts. 

The Dolphins kept the Vikings out of the end zone and were able to get on the board for sacks.  But they will face much better QBs and offenses in the next few games and they don’t appear to have solved the issue of keeping QBs from getting easy completions.  They also couldn’t get off the field when they needed to.

If I asked you how many plays the Dolphins had in the fourth quarter, could you tell me without looking it up?  I’ll tell you now: 3. That’s it.  Three plays was all the offense had.  We can argue about how bad the offense was and argue about where Willis should have thrown the ball on his final attempt.  What we REALLY need to discuss is the fact that Minnesota got the ball at the end of the 3rd quarter – running one play in the 3rd – went on a 14 play drive to get a FG, leaving Miami with 6:41 on the clock.  Miami went 3-and-out and that’s bad.  But Minnesota got the ball back with 5:48 left and proceeded to end the game with a 10-play drive that should have ended with a TD, but they had 3 more plays to kneel out the game.  Miami’s offense was bad. But Miami’s defense allowed Minnesota to run 26 plays – 26 FREAKING PLAYS – and burn 14 minutes in the FOURTH QUARTER ALONE!!!  We can whine about the OL and QB play and all of that until the cows come home.  But another easy way to help the QB is for the defense to GET. OFF. THE. FIELD!  That was an embarrassment.

THIS AND THAT

  • They say football is a game of inches, but in this contest, it was a game of millimeters.  Or perhaps microns.  Malik Willis and Chris Bell had a highlight reel TD play wiped off the board because Bell’s toenail was across the line out of bounds.  The Dolphins were going to get a first down due to roughing the kicker, but the defender got a fingernail on the ball to tip it.  Ollie Gordon was “touched down” on a run despite the replay showing the defender merely wafted in his general direction.  That negated what would have been a big run, possibly a TD run.  All of these were game-changing plays that could have been the difference in the outcome.  The toe being out of bounds cost a TD. The tipped punt that could have extended a drive resulted in a FG drive for Minnesota.  That’s a 10-point swing in a game decided by 5 points.  Not to mention the possible TD run stolen from Gordon.  The discussion about the Dolphins offense is different today if the final was say… 24-20 in Miami’s favor.
  • The officials were WAY too prevalent in this game.  This isn’t a complaint about Miami getting screwed, although that argument could be made.  Minnesota had more penalties than the Dolphins.  There was a total of 20: 9 for Miami, 11 for Minnesota.  That’s way too much laundry on the field for an NFL.  There were other officiating issues across the league.  It has become a very visible problem.  I would say in this game, it was due to 2 crappy offenses more than anything else.  But fans across the league are taking notice. Not only that, but two officials, including the referee for the Dolphins game have been suspended by the league for conduct towards players on Sunday.
  • Ollie Gordon II had his breakout game, and he should be the starter moving forward.  Last week, I was going to write about how OG2 seems to struggle with vision and doesn’t have the burst needed to be a full-time starter.  But I waited to see what he’d do in this game.  He ended up with 100 yards even on 9 carries.  Most of that came on a 53 jaunt early in the third quarter.  As usge, I like to exclude a long run or pass play from the stats (or a long negative play) because it can skew the averages, making something that’s actually negative look like a positive.  I shall name this “The Kalen Ballage Rule”.  Going 100 yards on 9 carries is an 11.1 YPC average and looks nice.  But excluding the 53-yard run, he went 47 yards on 8 carries for a 5.9 YPC average.  Which is also nice.  That means he was effective overall despite one stat-skewing play.  One of those 8 runs also included the aforementioned play where he was “touched down” when he could have had many more yards.  I’m not sure what’s going on with Wright, but Gordon is clearly better right now.  He runs angry and with power.  My biggest concern is ball security.  He was carrying the ball way too loosely for my preference when going into traffic.  If I saw it, you know DCs see it.  Put both hands on the ball Ollie!
  • The pass rush came to play with Sieler breaking out of the slump.  I thought he murdered Murray on one play.  Chop earned his sack with an awesome bull rush where he mauled the RT.  Uche is playing well also, to the point he might become an extension candidate.  I’m not gonna count those chickens just yet, but the edge guys are coming alive.  Chop is getting a lot of attention also.  He is getting doubled.  He’s not going to win every rep – no edge rusher does – but teams are wary of his presence.  They just need another inside presence.  Phillips is a good NT, but his pass rushing skills aren’t there right now.  Biggers is looking more and more like a depth player.  When Grant returns, perhaps he can provide some interior rush to go along with Sieler.  If he can provide it, the defense might be ready to take the next step.
  • I see you, Rodney McGraw.  He only played 12 defensive snaps, but I noticed him on a few.  I’ve always been a sucker for the underdog types in the NFL.  Cam Wake has always been my favorite player because of his story.  I will always root for guys like Sieler and Nik Needham, Kader Kohou, and now McGraw.  I don’t know if he’ll get many more opportunities, but I hope he does.  At 6’4”, 273, he can be a bigger edge player that Hafley seems to like.  Malik Herring is also in that mix.  He played 28 snaps and it is getting about 25 snaps per game.  Could he be another waiver claim gem like Sieler once was?  He seems like he’s developing into a quality run defender.

I SAID WHAT I SAID

I don’t see many opportunities for wins on the schedule this season and this game was one of them.  The Dolphins squandered it away and now come home to face a much better offense in the Bengals.  More on that later in the week.  Anyway, there seems to be a couple of bright spots every week, even in the midst of negativity.  They just need something to bring it all together.  Anyone have a cardboard cutoff of Rachel Phelps?

item.title: The good and the bad about the Chiefs’ win against the Raiders
item.description: Two defensive players highlighted a big win on the road for Kansas City.
item.content:encoded:
That was a great football game. The Kansas City Chiefs and the Las Vegas Raiders have often been a lopsided rivalry for the Chiefs, but the Raiders came into this game 3-0 and wanted to prove themselves. And to their credit, they showed up and competed. This game was a haymaker, with both sides having impressive moments, and the Chiefs ultimately made the timely plays to close it out.

There’s a lot to be impressed with in this game, but let’s focus on two players that set the tone defensively:

George Karlaftis’s impressive performance

Kirk Cousins wasn’t sacked in this game, which might lead you to think the Chiefs’ defensive line didn’t get much pressure. However, the Chiefs did get pressure on Cousins in this game 34.6% of his dropbacks, which was 16th in the NFL for Week 4. Without blitzes, the Chiefs were 12th at 34.2%.

Two players led the charge in getting pressure in this game: defensive ends R Mason Thomas and George Karlaftis. Thomas finished the day with eight pressures, including five in the fourth quarter. Thomas took time to get into this game, but his speed and explosiveness off the edge showed up when it mattered.

But for me, the most impressive performance for the Chiefs defense was Karlaftis. Karlaftis brought it all four quarters and did it on a higher snap count against the Raiders’ better tackle, left tackle Kolton Miller.

Karlaftis isn’t always the most reliable pass rusher turning the corner, but he did it in this game. Here, he uses his hands to swipe down the tackle’s outside arm, then uses his speed to turn the corner and nearly get to the quarterback before he checks it down.

Karlaftis establishing himself as a cornering threat opened up other pass rush moves, including this speed-to-power bull rush. Karlaftis flies off the ball and flashes that he’s trying to get upfield, which gets the tackle to subtly open his hip upfield. Karlaftis then turns toward the quarterback and attacks the tackle’s inside foot, which isn’t planted. Without that anchor foot established, it’s an easy run through for Karlaftis to get the pressure.

Karlaftis did a very good job in this game, continuing to work late into the down to get off tackles, particularly going inside. His balance and torque were impressive. He got Miller to lean his upper body forward, which put him in a bad position to recover. Karlaftis could then work inside, using his inside hand to attack Miller’s inside shoulder and create separation. He did this 3-4 times this game, and it worked.

Mansoor Delane’s impact as a run defender

Mansoor Delane has been impressive as a rookie in many departments. He’s looked good in man coverage for the most part, sticking to receivers. When the Chiefs play zone coverage, Delane shows off impressive click-and-close and route recognition.

However, what’s impressed me most about Delane so far is his play as a run defender. Delane has racked up 10 tackles in two straight games, and a lot of those plays are run stops. For a sub-190-pound player, that is impressive.

The Raiders often ran condensed formations, which force corners into the run fit. They run a short-side toss here with the WR responsible to crack Delane. Delane sees this and gets outside the block, forces Ashton Jeanty back inside, and makes an impressive one-on-one tackle.

Another short-side toss here, but Delane is now the furthest player to the edge, responsible for setting it. Delane strings out the run and keeps the running back from getting the angle on the sideline. If he can’t set an edge there, the running back beats Nick Bolton to the edge and that turns into a chunk run.

This was a massive run stop by Delane that saved at least an explosive run, if not a house call. The Raiders call a counter play, shifting their third tight end and pulling their right guard. Tranquill flies too far upfield, Bolton gets caught, and Chamarri Conner gets pinned and falls over. Delane is the only free defender near the line of scrimmage. If he misses this tackle, the only guy left is Alohi Gilman one-on-one with a two-way go. Delane makes an incredibly clutch tackle that prevents an explosive run.

The third-and-eight play call to end the game

For the most part, I thought the Chiefs played and executed a fairly clean game, but what bothered me most was Andy Reid’s decision to pass on third and eight on the Chiefs’ last offensive drive. The Raiders had no timeouts with around ninety seconds left. If the Chiefs had run the ball, they would’ve been able to get the clock down to around 35-40 seconds. Instead, by throwing the ball and having it go incomplete, the Chiefs gave the Raiders a free forty seconds.

To be fair to Reid, Matt Araiza had a great punt to get the Raiders downed at the 1, and Araiza had a great game punting even before that. Realistically, your defense should be able to get a stop there, which they did. However, the Raiders were knocking on field goal range with no timeouts.

The Raiders offense played decently throughout the game, but they struggled to push the ball downfield, especially when forced to do it in obvious passing situations. If they had 40 fewer seconds to run their last drive, I just don’t think they could’ve picked up enough yards in time to get close.

If this was a big playoff game against an elite quarterback, I totally understand giving Mahomes the ball to close the game, but in that specific context, you have to keep the clock running. Credit Araiza for the punt and the defense for coming through.

item.title: Sean McVay says Rams' coaches need to "get the hell out of the way" after sideline penalty
item.description: Rams quarterbacks coach Dave Ragone got a 15-yard penalty for unsportsmanlike conduct on Sunday after he stood too close to the field and collided with an official who was running down the sideline.
item.content:encoded:
Rams quarterbacks coach Dave Ragone got a 15-yard penalty for unsportsmanlike conduct on Sunday after he stood too close to the field and collided with an official who was running down the sideline. Rams coach Sean McVay says that can't happen.

When talking about some of the mistakes the Rams made in the first three quarters before turning things around and beating the Eagles with a fourth-quarter comeback, McVay noted that the coaches aren't exempt from the criticism that the team hasn't been focused enough at times.

"Focus, concentration and situational awareness, we have to do a better job on that," McVay said. "When it rains, it pours. Shoot, we’re getting penalties on our staff now too. Thank God we won that one. Rags would have never lived that one down. He felt bad about that one. So he took great accountability. We'll get everybody the hell out of the way. And I need to get the hell out of the way as well.”

It was one of several costly penalties for the Rams, who were flagged eight times for 100 penalty yards. They won the game, but McVay wants to make sure everyone, players and coaches alike, knows that can't happen.

item.title: Getting Defensive: Week 5 fantasy plays led by Vikings, Jaguars; top streaming defenses
item.description: Gary Davenport breaks down the fantasy football defense landscape headed into Week 5 of the 2026 NFL season.
item.content:encoded:
Confession time: This writer has a soft spot for ultra-aggressive defenses. Whether it was Buddy Ryan’s “46” in the in the 1980s with the Chicago Bears or Dick LeBeau’s “Blitzburgh” zone-blitz scheme the following decade, I love defenses that act, not react. That set the tempo for a game.

Yes, there are more recent examples, I’m old. Let me reminisce.

The most recent example would be Brian Flores’ defense in Minnesota. The Vikings don’t have constant five-man fronts like Ryan or send a safety while dropping a defensive tackle like LeBeau. Schematically, it’s a fairly straightforward setup with a 4-3 base and a lot of two-high nickel sets.

What sets the Vikings apart is Flores’ affinity for heating opposing quarterbacks up. Minnesota blitzes over 70 percent of the time—a staggering number when you consider no other team sends an extra guy over half the time. It’s not a matter of if the Vikings are coming—it’s a matter of how many.

That aggressiveness is helping fantasy managers, too. One month into the season the Vikings are fantasy’s highest-scoring defense. Minnesota is fifth in the league in total defense, seventh against both the pass and the run, first in scoring defense and sacks and tied for third in the league in takeaways.

Is that good? It sounds good.

Fantasy Football Waiver Wire Week 5: Emanuel Wilson takes over in Seattle
Emanuel Wilson broke out in Week 4 with 120 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns. The Seahawks running back headlines the list of top fantasy football waiver wire adds for Week 5.
  • Kyle Dvorchak,

THE NO-DOUBTERS

Minnesota Vikings (at New Orleans Saints)

If Monday night’s loss to the Atlanta Falcons is any indication, the Saints offense has problems. The team that couldn’t run the ball before Travis Etienne got hurt is lost now on the ground, and asking Tyler Shough to drop back 50 times against the Minnesota pass rush on Sunday isn’t conducive to his living to see Monday. The Saints have shown improvement at times this year, but they remain a flawed squad that has been hit hard by injuries. The Vikings will still be the top fantasy defense a week from now.

Jacksonville Jaguars (vs. Philadelphia Eagles)

That’s right—the Jaguars are a no-doubt, lock that in fantasy start this week at home against the Philadelphia Eagles. The Jaguars are quietly second in fantasy points among defenses, and in their two games at Everbank Stadium Jacksonville has been outright dominant, outscoring two visitors (each .500 or better) 69-16. Meanwhile, the Eagles could be without Saquon Barkley. And DeVonta Smith. And Dallas Goedert. And right tackle Lane Johnson. The Eagles have, as they say, issues. Avail yourself of them.

Pittsburgh Steelers (vs. Indianapolis Colts)

The Steelers have cooled off a bit defensively after a hot start to the season, but they still sit in a familiar spot—among the top-five defenses in fantasy points. The Colts have won two straight, but beating a Commanders team led by a rookie third-string quarterback doesn’t exactly impress. The biggest takeaway in Indy over the season’s first month is that Daniel Jones is about as mobile as a lamppost. Given Pittsburgh’s formidable pass rush, that’s going to be a problem for the Colts in Week 5.

Denver Broncos (at Los Angeles Chargers)

Last year’s elite defenses have demonstrated why you can’t trust a defense from one year to the next. The Broncos haven’t stumbled as badly as the Houston Texans over the first month of the season, but statistically speaking they are well off last year’s pace. With that said, the Chargers have gone from contender to tomato can—and the 0-4 Bolts have given up the second-most fantasy points to defenses this year. The Chargers are a dumpster fire. Get warm.

Chicago Bears (at Green Bay Packers)

That the Bears have remained an offensive buzzsaw despite starting three different quarterbacks in four games is garnering most of the run, and rightly so. But the last couple of weeks, the Bears have been rolling on defense as well, ranking inside the top-five in fantasy points over that span. Meanwhile, the Packers are floundering offensively, especially on the ground—the team’s 86 yards last week was a season-high. The Packers have also allowed the ninth-most fantasy points to defenses in 2026. Lambeau ain’t saving this team this time against these Bears.

Houston Texans (at Tennessee Titans)

That the Texans are 0-4 is surprising in and of itself. But the reason why is a stunner. One of the NFL’s best defenses a year ago has been a shell of that unit this year—Houston has the fifth-worst pass defense in the league and has allowed the sixth-most points per contest. But if you’ve sunk the cost and rode Houston this far despite the team barely ranking inside the top-20 in fantasy points, you can’t give up now—the Titans have next to no offense and have been kind to opposing defenses this season.

STREAMERS OF THE WORLD, UNITE!

Cincinnati Bengals (at Miami Dolphins)

The Bengals have dropped two straight, the first of which was an ugly defensive performance in Pittsburgh. But Cincinnati appears to have accomplished that which the Cowboys aspired to—the Bengals defense isn’t Ryan’s Bears (Mike Ditka just swore at me), but they have been better than last year’s mess. A top-five ranking in points for the year is born of one massive week more than their prowess, but a plus fantasy matchup in Miami gets the Bengals on the streaming radar this week. Who Dey and all that.

New York Giants (at Washington Commanders)

The Giants are somehow in first place in the NFC East despite losing starting quarterback Jaxson Dart, and the defense has played a significant role—the Giants are seventh in fantasy points at the position, and while they haven’t had any huge games they also haven’t laid any eggs. Now Big Blue heads to Washington to take on a Commanders team that can’t run the ball who will as likely as not be starting Athan Kaliakmanis at quarterback. He’s a real person. Or so I found out last Sunday.

Cleveland Browns (at New York Jets)

This Browns defense isn’t as dominant as last year, but they are rounding into shape. Take away the Week 1 debacle in Jacksonville and Cleveland has been steady—steady enough to rank inside the top-five since Week 2. Meanwhile, the Jets appear to be headed toward another Jets season—last week New York had fewer total yards than their opponent had on the ground. With Breece Hall more likely than not sitting another week (at least), the Jets are going to struggle to move the ball again. Forcing Geno Smith to take chances is good for fantasy defenses.

Dallas Cowboys (vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers)

Remember when the Cowboys were going to be better defensively this season? Those were fun times. It’s also clearly fallacy—a month into the season the Cowboys are a bottom-10 defense in terms of yards allowed and a bottom-five defense in terms of points allowed. The thing is, this week at least, it doesn’t matter—the winless Buccaneers have surrendered more fantasy points to defenses than any team in the NFL, and Tampa will be starting an undrafted rookie under center on the road on a short week.

CAVEAT EMPTOR, FOLKS!

Seattle Seahawks (vs. San Francisco 49ers)

This is one of those matchups where the course of action is dictated by record. If your fantasy team is 2-2 or better and you have the Seahawks rostered (not like they’re sitting on waiver wires), then roll ‘em out like any other week—with the expectation that their output will be less than average. But if you have come out of the gate slow and are point-scrounging, it’s a far tougher call. Brock Purdy doesn’t get sacked. Or make many mistakes with the ball. Some people have no consideration for others.

item.title: Fantasy Football: It's officially time to panic over the entire Eagles offense
item.description: Fantasy football analyst Ray Garvin unveils the Panic Meter ahead of Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
At this point, I'm not really interested in explaining away four weeks of bad offense. The Panic Meter is still simple: No Panic, Some Panic, Total Panic or Coping Corner. But Philadelphia has moved past the point where I can call this a slow start, a new scheme problem or an injury-created dip.

This offense has been stuck in neutral for a while now. Philadelphia Eagles offense: TOTAL PANIC.

This is not just about losing two straight games.

This is about what the offense has looked like for an extended stretch, including the end of last season. The Eagles hired Sean Mannion to modernize the passing game, blend in more of the McVay and Shanahan concepts and give Jalen Hurts more answers in the middle of the field.

So far? I'm not seeing it.

Philadelphia is averaging 269.8 yards per game, 29th in the NFL. The Eagles are 30th in passing yards at 178.3 per game, 27th in third-down conversion rate at 35.8% and 25th in scoring at 18.8 points per game.

Then you get to the drive-level stuff.

The Eagles have already gone three-and-out 15 times, the most in the NFL. Eleven of those three-and-outs have come in the second half, also the most in football by a wide margin. They just went 0-for-12 on third down against the Rams, Philadelphia's most third-down attempts without a conversion since at least 1991.

That is not a functioning offense.

The 172 total yards against Los Angeles were the Eagles' fewest in a game since 2014. Jalen Hurts threw for 93 yards. Philadelphia scored 20 points because the defense and special teams kept handing the offense short fields.

The box score lied. And honestly, a lot of the offseason talk feels like it lied, too.

We spent months hearing about how the offense was going to marry the run and pass game better, how the under-center package would help create play-action answers and how Hurts would have more opportunities attacking the middle of the field. That was the sales pitch.

Historically, Hurts has targeted the short middle of the field on only 8.3% of his pass attempts compared to a league average of 14.5%. On intermediate middle throws, he has been at 4.6% compared to a 7.4% league average.

The whole idea was that the new structure would open that area up. Instead, Philadelphia still looks like an offense searching for easy answers it cannot find.

Hurts is averaging 16.8 fantasy points through four games. His weekly totals are 24.7, 16.2, 12.6 and 13.5. That is not disastrous fantasy production, but it is nowhere close to what you paid for.

More importantly, I do not like how he is getting there.

The rushing floor is smaller. The passing volume is not creating enough yardage. The offense is constantly behind schedule. When you are 30th in passing yards and one of the worst third-down teams in football, there are just not enough sustained drives for everybody to eat.

That is the bigger fantasy problem.

Saquon Barkley has 36 carries for 182 yards through four games with no rushing touchdowns and only four receptions. Yes, the Week 4 hamstring injury changes the evaluation. But the larger issue was already there before he got hurt. The Eagles are not creating enough clean scoring opportunities.

DeVonta Smith is still the pass-catcher I trust most. He had 27 targets through his first three games with 19 catches, 235 yards and a touchdown before missing Week 4. If he gets healthy, the role is good enough. But Dallas Goedert's knee still isn't right. Makai Lemon is not a stash for me in normal Yahoo leagues. He is running routes, but that has not translated into meaningful opportunity. His route participation is 81.1%, yet he owns only a 10.2% target share, an 11.3% first-read target share and 8.7% of Philadelphia's air yards. That is a cardio role.

I do not need to stash the fourth or fifth option in the 30th-ranked passing offense waiting for everything around him to suddenly become functional.

Could Philadelphia get healthier and improve? Sure. But I do not want to hear that as the explanation for everything.

The offense was already in need of a reset coming out of last season. Mannion was brought in to provide one. Four weeks in, Philadelphia is 29th in total offense, 30th in passing and leading the NFL in three-and-outs.

At some point, you stop calling it a slow start. This is just who they are right now.

Total Panic.

Justin Herbert, QB, Chargers: TOTAL PANIC

Mike McDaniel was supposed to be the elixir. The whole idea was simple: take one of the most physically gifted quarterbacks in football, give him a creative offensive mind and finally make life easier for him.

It has not happened.

The Chargers are averaging 16.8 points per game, 29th in the NFL. They rank 23rd in passing yards at 204 per game and 21st in total offense.

Herbert has thrown exactly one touchdown in every game. Four games. Four touchdowns. Six interceptions. His fantasy totals are 13.3, 7.9, 12.7 and 9.6. That is 10.9 points per game.

The scheme has not fixed the protection problem either. Herbert has been pressured on 34.6% of his dropbacks and has already taken 12 sacks, three per game. The Chargers' offensive pressure rate over expected ranks 27th in the NFL, meaning this is not just Herbert holding the football too long and creating his own problems.

The offensive line is still getting beat. That is the part I keep coming back to.

McDaniel can draw up all the motion, spacing and misdirection he wants. If the quarterback is still getting hit, the offense is still losing early downs and Herbert is still being asked to bail everything out, then how much actually changed?

Herbert is averaging only 204 passing yards per game despite 119 attempts. That is 6.9 yards per attempt.

There has not been enough explosiveness, there have not been enough touchdowns and there definitely has not been enough fantasy production.

I still believe Herbert is a very good quarterback. But fantasy does not grade quarterback talent. You drafted him to score points. Right now he is not doing it.

Total Panic.

TreVeyon Henderson, RB, Patriots: TOTAL PANIC

I keep waiting for the TreVeyon Henderson fantasy breakout. New England keeps telling us to stop waiting.

Henderson has 38 carries for 141 yards through three active games. He has three targets and one reception. Three targets — that is the part fantasy managers need to sit with.

The explosive receiving-back profile we thought would protect his floor has basically disappeared.

His 39-yard touchdown run in Week 2 is also doing a lot of work for the rushing line. Take that play away and Henderson has 37 carries for 102 yards. That is 2.8 yards per carry.

His backfield usage tells the same story.

Henderson owns only 29.1% of New England's running back utilization and 34.8% of the running back rush share. Both sit around 40th among NFL backs. That is not a featured workload.

Rhamondre Stevenson continues to get the valuable snaps, the passing-down work and the goal-line opportunities. He scored from the one-yard line again in Week 4 while Henderson finished with 14 carries for 42 yards and 4.2 fantasy points.

This is where I have to start questioning the fantasy assumption we made about Henderson. Maybe he is not some future 70% backfield player waiting for the Patriots to figure it out. Maybe he is really good in a complementary role.

That does not mean he is a bad player. It does not mean he cannot rip off another 40-yard touchdown next week.

It means there is a major difference between being an explosive NFL weapon and being a fantasy running back we can trust every Sunday.

Right now, Henderson needs the big play because the role is not giving him enough anywhere else. That is Total Panic.

George Pickens, WR, Cowboys: SOME PANIC

There is no real mystery here. This offense runs through CeeDee Lamb. He is Dallas' best wide receiver and when the Cowboys decide the answer is feeding him, George Pickens is going to have weeks where there simply is not enough left.

Week 4 was the perfect example. Lamb saw 21 targets, Pickens saw three.

Lamb caught 17 passes for 189 yards and a touchdown. Pickens caught two passes for 75 yards. That is the entire Pickens experience right now.

The good news is the season-long usage is still strong. Pickens owns a 23.8% target share. Lamb is also at 23.8%. Pickens has 35.2% of Dallas' air yards and a 29.3% first-read target share. Those are good numbers.

The Cowboys are also feeding wide receivers more than almost any team in football. Dallas has sent 71.5% of its targets to wide receivers, the second-highest rate in the NFL. There is enough passing volume for two receivers to produce here.

The problem is the hierarchy.

Lamb has a 30.7% first-read share compared to Pickens at 29.3%. Lamb owns 41% of the team's air yards compared to 35.2% for Pickens. His weighted opportunity rating is also higher.

It is not some gigantic gap, but it is enough to tell you who this offense is built around.

Pickens has 28 targets, 18 catches, 225 yards and no touchdowns through four games.

The zero touchdowns will correct at some point. The weekly target volatility might not. That is why I am at Some Panic instead of Total Panic.

Pickens still has a strong role inside one of the most receiver-heavy passing games in football. But fantasy managers drafted him hoping he would function like a weekly WR1.

As long as Lamb is healthy, I do not think that is the right expectation.

Colston Loveland, TE, Bears: SOME PANIC

Loveland is the one player on this list where the arrow has actually started moving in the right direction.

The beginning of the season was brutal. Two targets in Week 1. Three in Week 2. Four in Week 3. Then he saw nine in Week 4.

Loveland caught six passes for 57 yards and finished with 8.7 half-PPR points. It was not some monster breakout, but it was finally a game where the opportunity matched what fantasy managers expected when they drafted him.

There are still reasons to keep expectations in check. His season-long target share is only 9.2% and he owns just 7.2% of Chicago's air yards. Those are not top-three fantasy tight end numbers.

Chicago also has a crowded passing game. The Bears have sent 61.2% of their targets to wide receivers and 24.8% to tight ends, so there is enough volume at the position for Loveland to matter, but he still has to earn a larger slice of it consistently.

The route participation is encouraging. Loveland is running a route on 72.8% of Chicago's dropbacks, eighth among tight ends. That gives him a chance. The nine targets give me a little more hope.

I do not think we are getting the top-three fantasy tight end season people drafted in August. That dream probably needs to go. But the player has been better, the target trend is moving in the right direction and Week 4 finally gave us a reason for some small level of optimism.

That is enough to move him from Total Panic to Some Panic.

item.title: Bijan Robinson, Kenneth Walker III should be serious MVP candidates
item.description: The MVP award has become, essentially, a "best quarterback" award — with rare exceptions.
item.content:encoded:
The MVP award has become, essentially, a "best quarterback" award — with rare exceptions.

No non-quarterback has won the MVP prize since Vikings running back Adrian Peterson eked out the distinction over Peyton Manning in 2012. In the current century, a non-quarterback became the MVP only four times: Marshall Faulk in 2000, Shaun Alexander in 2005, LaDainian Tomlinson in 2006, and Peterson in 2012.

This year, a couple of running backs deserve serious consideration, based on what we've seen through four weeks.

Falcons running back Bijan Robinson is a touchdown waiting to happen, on any given play. His opening-drive 59-yard touchdown run on Monday night in New Orleans set the tone for Atlantas' 45-24 win.

Though four games, Robinson has 494 yards rushing and 120 yards receiving and five total touchdowns.

Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III has become the straw that stirs the Kansas City cocktail. He has 537 yards rushing, 84 yards receiving, and six total touchdowns. He's also the third player in NFL history to have 170 or more rushing yards in two of the first four games of a season, joining only Jim Brown and O.J. Simpson.

Both Robinson and Walker have 99 touches. Walker has gained 621 yards. Robinson has gained 614.

When it comes to the MVP betting odds (which are instructive to the general perceptions that surely will influence some or many of the 50 Associated Press voters), both Robinson and Walker are low on the list. Robinson, who was 70-1 when Simms and I discussed the dynamic earlier this morning on PFT Live, is now at 60-1. Walker is 50-1.

Currently, the eight highest players on the list of odds are quarterbacks.

Lions running back Jahmyr Gibbs sits at 30-1, which may be a reflection of the bets made on him before the season started. (He has 102 touches and 540 yards from scrimmage, with seven touchdowns.)

Here's the real question. Is the perception of "value" skewed by the fact that the best quarterbacks make so much more money than the best quarterbacks? The top of the quarterback market is approaching $65 million per year. Gibbs, the highest-paid running back, is at $22.5 million annually.

Robinson sits at $22.25 million per year. Walker, who signed as a free agent months before the Robinson and Gibbs deals were done, is making $14.35 million per year. (To put it apples-to-apples terms, the Gibbs deal is worth $16.995 million per year from signing, Robinson’s deal has an average of $16.36 million from signing.)

The best running backs are far more valuable to their teams than the market suggests. The existing market held back Walker, Robinson, and Gibbs. The enhanced injury risk at the position is a major factor in the unwillingness of teams to embrace the financial risk that the player at some point won't be available.

While their "value" may not properly be reflected in their contracts, it needs to be recognized in their consideration for the MVP award. The present betting trends show that it's not. Whether it will be comes down to the ability and willingness of the voters to stop viewing the MVP as a quarterback prize and to start looking at the definition of the prize, as articulated by the AP.

"The player who was most valuable to their team over the course of the season."

Robinson and Walker fit the bill. Gibbs will, too, if the Lions can recover from a sluggish start and become true contenders.
