item.title: The Hot Read: The Buffalo Bills need to grow up
item.description: The Bills cannot keep repeating their same mistakes.
item.content:encoded:
The Bills are still the Bills. In some ways, that makes them one of the NFL’s best teams. In other ways, it scares their fans to death.

This season was supposed to be one of transformation for Buffalo. Unfortunately for Bills Mafia, Sunday was a sign that the more things change, the more they stay the same. After a 3-0 start and entering a game in which they could have put an early kill shot into the New England Patriots, the Bills instead allowed their division rivals to not just win, but find their groove.

The Patriots had just 19 points on the season entering the Week 4 matchup; they scored 29 points against the Bills’ defense – a unit new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard was expected to make better. What has transpired has been a defense that ranks 30th in EPA per play, has allowed the second-most touchdown passes in the league, and the seventh-most points in the league. No one was expecting the Bills to be the best defense in the NFL, but to be statistically one of the worst is just more of the same that fans saw with Sean McDermott and Bobby Babich.

Offensively, Joe Brady went away from everything that worked in the first three weeks. The Bills had the third-highest EPA per play in 12 personnel in Weeks 1-3, yet they only ran nine such plays against the Patriots. James Cook was averaging over six yards per carry, but only ran the ball 12 times. Brady even reverted back to eye-roll-worthy calls with a screen on 3rd-and-8 that was sniffed out and led to a punt. Dalton Kincaid was fourth in EPA per target among tight ends with at least 50 routes run entering Week 4 – he had two targets. Why the Bills diverted from everything that helped them start 3-0 was as concerning as it was familiar.

And while Brady and Leonard shoulder most of the blame, Josh Allen isn’t without fault. Despite all the aforementioned shortcomings, with just over a minute to play and all three timeouts still in his back pocket, Allen dodged a sack and launched a pass into double coverage to Josh Palmer, which was picked off by Craig Woodson. Allen could have taken off and got a modest gain, hit the check down, which was open to the right, or tried extending the play even longer to allow something to develop.

Yes, his defense didn’t play well, and yes he gave them the lead with less than five minutes left in the game on an absolute rope of a pass to Keon Coleman. All of that can be acknowledged while also saying that we are now in Year Nine of Allen’s career, and you can still set your watch to a postgame press conference where he looks distraught following an incredibly immature throw that he has no business trying. Think back to 2022 when he threw a pair of red zone interceptions agains the Vikings, the second of which came in overtime on a heavily contested throw when an underneath check down was wide open. Or Week 1 of the 2023 season agains the New York Jets that featured three picks in a loss to a Jets team that was led by Zach Wilson after Aaron Rodgers went down with an Achilles injury.

“Same s—it, same place, different day,” Allen said after that 2023 opener.

Now Sunday, when he had all the tools and time to get Buffalo at minimum into field goal range, and at maximum in the end zone to get to a 4-0 start. After the game, he once again took responsibility for a horrid decision that ultimately cost his team. And look, man. It’s great that he is willing to take responsibility for his mistakes. But at some point, he needs to be smarter in these moments. Every team loses, no one is saying the Bills need to go 17-0. But these are the types of losses that end up costing you. Last year, the Bills lost to the Falcons and Dolphins, two teams that fired their head coach and started anew in 2026. Had they won both of those games, they finish the year 14-3 and as the potential No. 1 seed in the AFC. So should they finish with a 12-5 record and a game out of the No. 1 seed this season, or should the Patriots battle back to win the AFC East, this game will certainly haunt them.

None of this is to say that all of a sudden Josh Allen is to blame for all the Bills’ issues – he’s not. Nor is it to take away from the once in a lifetime talent that he is or to downplay his greatness. It’s merely saying the Bills need to grow up. Joe Brady needs to show he isn’t Sean McDermott and make real changes to the defensive personnel. Jim Leonhard has to tighten up a unit that, outside of its front four, has been incredibly disappointing and easy to dissect. And Allen needs to be smarter and more mature with his decision-making in the game’s biggest moments. Because in order to finally get over that proverbial hump, he and his teammates have to show that the Bills aren’t still the Bills.

That was the cold open. This is the Hot Read.

Three and out

The Broncos don’t trust Bo Nix

Actions speak louder than words, and the Denver Broncos are telling you they don’t believe in their quarterback. Bo Nix finished the Broncos’ Week 4 loss to the San Francisco 49ers going 25-of-42 for 214 yards and a touchdown. Of those 25 completions, only six travelled further than five yards downfield. Additionally, Nix has an average depth of target of just 6.01 yards, and his average air yards to sticks is -3.48 yards, meaning his average throw is about 3.5 yards short of where the first down marker is – both of those numbers are the lowest in the NFL among 33 quarterbacks who have at least 50 dropbacks. His short passing percentage also sits at 77 percent, which leads the NFL.

These are not the tendencies of a team that believes they have the right guy under center who can make splash plays downfield. I referenced his six passes downfield, but seeing his Week 4 passing chart really puts into perspective how the Broncos play offense – scared.

Swing passes, screen passes, underneath quick passes – that’s what you do when you have little faith in your quarterback. And it’s hard to blame Sean Payton and offensive coordinator Davis Webb, because Nix hasn’t been good. He has a lower EPA per play than Jacoby Brissett, per Sumer Sports, and a lower success rate than Cam Ward. And I hate to say I told you so, only no, I actually love to say that – but I’ve said this about Nix since he entered the league. This is the type of play he put on tape at Auburn and Oregon. And while the underneath passes and screens helped open up the deep passing game a year ago, it hasn’t this season, as Nix is 21st in the league in EPA per play on deep passes. Teams are also realizing that if you pressure Nix, he crumbles, as he is 26th in pass success rate when facing pressure.

This is what Nix is – a middle of the pack quarterback at his absolute best, and a bottom-dweller starter at worst. The Broncos’ defense hasn’t been its elite self through four games either, and they need to be borderline perfect to win games when the offense is this bad. This iteration of the Broncos peaked last season and rode a magic carpet to the AFC Championship – they won’t come close to those heights again.

The Atlanta Falcons might be a wagon

Where the hell did this come from? Over the last two weeks, the Falcons have erupted offensively, and they’ve done so largely on the ground. In Weeks 3 and 4, the Falcons lead the NFL in EPA per play, and their 0.28 EPA per rush is astoundingly higher than the second-place Colts, who put up a 0.1 mark. Their success rate of 58.2 percent is also nearly a full five percent higher than the Detroit Lions (53.8) and their 447 rushing yards. On top of that, they are also first in rushing yards, rushing touchdowns, and yards after contact.

This corresponds with the return of Michael Penix, who has played very well in his own right. He’s averaging 10.6 yards per attempt with four touchdowns in two games. Turns out that your offense can be pretty good when Cooper Rush and Jack Strand aren’t your quarterbacks. Who would have guessed? And after a dreadful 0-2 start, the Falcons are all of a sudden the hottest offense in the NFL, and their Week 5 Sunday night matchup with the Baltimore Ravens is all of a sudden very intriguing.

The Houston Texans’ identity has become its impotence

Coming into the year, many proclaimed the Houston Texans’ defense to be the best in football, and there was certainly an easy argument to make. The were second in defensive EPA per play last season and second in success rate, as well. This season? A very different story.

Through four games, the Texans are 24th in defensive EPA per play, and they are allowing the third-most passing yards in the league. It’s not just the counting stats that show the obvious fall off from this unit over the last year, it’s their inability to close games. C.J. Stroud and the offense gave the Texans the lead with just over two minutes remaining, They held up their end of the bargain and then some. Stroud threw for 347 yards and two touchdowns, both of which were thrown to a returning Nico Collins. The defense answered that by allowing the Cowboys to drive 73 yards in 11 plays which ended with CeeDee Lamb catching his 17th pass of the day in the end zone.

Houston has allowed 30+ points twice in the first four games – they allowed 30 points just once in 2025. What was once the backbone of the team has become the very thing that paralyzes them, and an 0-4 start has been the result.

One play that changed everything

The Kansas City Chiefs trailed the Las Vegas Raiders 19-17 with under four minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. Kenneth Walker rushed for a two-yard score to make it 24-19, but it’s the next play that completely swung the result. Raiders kick returner Dareke Young fumbled on the ensuing kickoff, which was recovered by Jack Cochrane of the Chiefs. On the first play of the ensuing drive, Walker scored once again to put the Chiefs up 30-19, and that would end up being what sealed the 30-23 win to get the Chiefs to 4-0.

Buy or sell

Buy: Chicago Bears defense

The great Aaron Schatz and his 2026 Football Almanac projected the Bears to have the worst defense in the league this season. Through four games, though, the Bears are holding their own. They are currently tied for fourth in defensive EPA per play, as well as being in the upper half in defensive success rate. They’ve also only allowed four passing touchdowns (second-fewest in the league), 282.3 yards per game (third-fewest in the league) and 65 points (fourth-fewest in the league). To continue, since Week 2, the Bears have allowed just 28 points – the fewest in the NFL in that span. Credit Dennis Allen for the job he’s done with a defense that lost five of its key players from a year ago. Not only is he making it work, but he’s making it thrive.

Sell: The Minnesota Vikings

Minnesota may be 4-0, but they are the John Daley standing across from Tiger Woods of 4-0 teams. The 49ers and Chiefs have been dominant offensively in their respective starts to the season, ranking second and fifth, respectively, in points scored and first and fourth in EPA per play while both of their defense rank in the top 12 in total yards allowed per game. The Vikings, while having the league’s top defense from an EPA and success rate perspective, have one of the league’s worst offenses. They are currently 31st in success rate, ahead of only the Dolphins. And some may point to Carson Wentz having to step in for a game and a half, but Kyler Murray hasn’t been good. In fact, from an efficiency standpoint, Wentz played better when starting. Of 41 quarterbacks to play at least 25 snaps this season, Murray is 38th in EPA per play and 39th in success rate while throwing just one touchdown to two interceptions. Their schedule is one where they can get to 10 wins from here based off what they’ve done so far, but if and when they get into the postseason, this isn’t a team that is a threat.

Buy: Rams resilience

We were less than a quarter away from talking about the Rams being 1-3 after being hyped as the easy Super Bowl favorites entering the season. But down 20-10 late in the third quarter, head coach Sean McVay gathered the offense in a sideline huddle and rallied his troops to start playing like the Rams we expected to see. Two Kyren Williams fourth-quarter touchdowns led Los Angeles back to complete a 10-point comeback on the road in Philadelphia, sending both teams to 2-2. It’s been an inconsistent start for the Rams, as Matthew Stafford is currently second in the NFL with six interceptions thrown. But this is a team that recognizes the season is a marathon, not a sprint. They’ll get Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald back. And once those two are next to each other, we’ll truly see if this Rams team can live up to its ungodly potential.

Sell: The New York Jets

I really believed the Jets would march into Solider Field and get a win over the Bears, and it’s not like that was a crazy thought. They had nearly defeated the Lions in Week 3, and should have beaten the Packers in Week 2. Instead what ensued was one of the most lopsided games in NFL history in terms of plays run and time of possession. The Bears ran 89 plays to just 32 for the Jets while holding the ball for 42:45. New York’s defense did get its first interception since 2024, but allowing the Bears to be on the field that long and completely control every aspect of the game is troubling. I fear this could be the game that sees the Jets revert back to the team we’ve come to know.

That said, they play the Browns in Week 5, so cut to next Tuesday where I look foolish after they give Cleveland its second loss.

Prediction to track

  • Week 1: Steelers will trade Joey Porter Jr: Correct
  • Week 2: Rams will beat Broncos handedly: Incorrect
  • Week 3: Lions will blowout Panthers: Incorrect

Alright, we’re going to take a break from predicting lopsided wins. Joey Porter Jr. did get dealt last week, though, so we’re on the board with our predictions. I’ll go back to the trade well and say that both Brian Thomas Jr. and Marvin Harrison Jr. are on new teams before the season ends. Both reached the end zone for the first time this season, but combined for just three catches in Week 4. On the year, the pair have combined for 14 catches and two touchdowns. Thomas has gone from 1,200 yards as a rookie to No. 4 option. Harrison has also found himself as the fourth option in the passing game behind Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne.

Both would be substantial targets in Baltimore, San Francisco, Las Vegas, and several other places. If neither of their current teams are going to use them, send them to squads who will.

item.title: Bills need to revert to highlighting tight end group on offense
item.description: The Bills need to get back to their bread and butter
item.content:encoded:
The Buffalo Bills were the talk of the NFL after the first two weeks of the season not only because they were averaging 38.5 points per game and started 2-0.

In the increasing analytics-happy or at least analytics aware NFL universe, Buffalo’s utilization of 13 personnel (three tight ends on the field at the same time) was applauded by the masses as the Bills standing away from the crowd — ironically alongside the Rams, their Week 5 opponent — to maximize offensive efficiency and keep defenses guessing run or pass.

The past two weeks, the heavy lean into 13 personnel has all but officially vanished.

The crazy part about the relatively very low rate in Week 4… of course DJ Moore left in the first half and didn’t return. That development was begging for the Bills to go revert to their previously trademark tight end trio, and they decided against it.

Also I can’t be convinced the Bills lack of 13 personnel against New England was game-script oriented. No team ever held more than a touchdown lead throughout.

The key piece to this group — Dalton Kincaid, only appeared on 35 snaps in Week 4, his first game under 40 snaps this season. For the Bills sake, it should be the only time he plays fewer than 40 snaps. His presence on the field is too valuable.

Sure, Kincaid isn’t going to move people in the run game like Dawson Knox or Jackson Hawes.

But if you’re sitting in a multiple tight-end set around 30-40% of the time, the opposition can’t always assume it’s a pass play. They have to match with more base defense with less coverageWhen it’s a hardly-used grouping, it doesn’t have nearly as much of a disguising effect.

If Moore can’t play against the Rams, the Bills need to live in multiple tight-end personnel groupings as much as reasonably possible. Doesn’t just have to be 13. Filter through the tight end combinations in 12 personnel. In fact, the Bills have dipped to 23rd in EPA per play when in 13 — the last two weeks have severely hurt those figures — but are 4th in EPA per play when using 12 personnel.

And this push isn’t simply schematic. Buffalo’s tight end trio needs to regularly block more effectively for the multiple-tight end sets to work well for the ground game too. Kincaid in particular.

Without Moore, the Bills should be shying away from 11 personnel (three receivers on the field). Without Moore, the receiver group is not a strength of the team.

The tight end group, running back, and offensive line are the strengths beyond Josh Allen.

Like Bruce wrote earlier today, the Bills need to look backwards to find answers to their problems.

Here’s to more multiple tight-end sets from the Bills on Monday Night Football against the Rams and in the foreseeable future.

While the Texas quarterback has had his moments since last season, he’s struggling when it matters most to some analysts. This is despite Manning having a solid stat line and leading the No. 1 team in the country right now.

But former QB Aaron Murray sees a different story. He only sees Arch Manning getting drafted high in 2027 (or 2028 for that matter) due to his last name and football lineage.

“As I look at NFL quarterbacks, especially guys get get drafted in the first round, they have some sort of elite characteristic about them,” Murray said on College Sports Radio on Sirius XM. “Even if they’re a little bit raw, something that an NFL coach can say like, man, like Josh Allen, for example. Josh Allen came out not very accurate as a quarterback in college, but the raw talent was there. We’re like, man, this guy’s got it, and I need that kind of raw talent or talent to win a Super Bowl, you know, for that position. And I just don’t think Arch has anything to me that screams this guy has the kind of talent that is a first round. Whether it’s arm strength, whether that’s elite athleticism … 

“He’s got a good arm. He’s a good athlete. He’s inconsistent with accuracy. But there’s nothing, to my point, that jumps off the page of like ‘we’re drafting him because he has this.’ People are going to draft him because he has the last name Manning. Not because he’s got a strong arm, not because he’s elite accuracy, not because he’s Lamar Jackson speed, because his last name’s Manning. Tell me, I’m wrong.” 

This year, Manning is 73-of-115 passing (63.5%) for 862 yards, seven touchdowns and three interceptions. He also has 82 rushing yards but no scores through four games, compared to 399 and 10 touchdowns last year.

item.title: NFL Week 5 betting: 5 biggest storylines, including the Bears as road favorites at Green Bay
item.description: There's only one team left that is undefeated against the spread this season.
item.content:encoded:
In Week 4, underdogs did quite well.

They went 11-5, with the Atlanta Falcons finishing it off with a big win as a small underdog against the New Orleans Saints. Both double-digit underdogs covered, though the Tennessee Titans nor the Miami Dolphins could pull off the upset win. Taking the points was the way to go in Week 4, though points weren't always needed. Seven underdogs won straight up.

Here are the top betting storylines for Week 5 of the NFL season:

Bears are rare favorites at Lambeau

The Bears are off to a hot start and the Packers have been wholly unimpressive. The surprise isn't that the Bears are favored in Green Bay, it's that it's less than a field goal.

The Bears are 2.5-point favorites against the Packers. It's the first time since 2006 that Chicago has been favored at Green Bay.

The Chicago Bears (-2.5) are currently a road favorite against the Green Bay Packers for the first time in 20 years.

➡️Last time Chicago was a favorite in GB was Week 1 of 2006 season (Bears -3.5, won 26-0)

— Ben Fawkes (@BFawkes22) October 5, 2026

The Packers-Bears rivalry hadn't been lively for many years, but then Ben Johnson showed up and made the Bears far more competitive. Two of their signature wins last season were a comeback against the Packers late in the regular season and a comeback win in the playoffs against Green Bay. The point spread for Week 5 shows how the rivalry has changed.

Can the Raiders cover again?

The Raiders are the only undefeated team against the spread left in the NFL this season. They didn't beat the Chiefs in Week 4, but they did cover a 4.5-point spread on a late touchdown by Brock Bowers.

The Raiders are getting the benefit of the doubt for this week. They're just a 3.5-point underdog at the New England Patriots, the reigning AFC champs who just beat the Bills straight up on the road in Week 4. That they're just a tick above a field goal for an early start on the East Coast against the Patriots shows that oddsmakers and the betting market respects the Raiders' start.

Who hasn't covered the spread yet?

There are still five teams that have yet to cover a spread this season, which is a pretty big number for four weeks into the season.

There are three teams that are 0-4 against the spread, according to Action Network: Texans, Eagles and Buccaneers. The Eagles and Bucs play standalone games this week. The Bucs are 8.5-point underdogs at the Cowboys on Thursday night, and the Eagles are +6.5 for a game against the Jaguars in London on Sunday morning.

Two other teams are 0-3-1 against the spread. The Lions and Chargers at least have covered once. That group of five is a pretty complete list of the most disappointing teams in the NFL so far this season.

No big spreads

It will be a little harder for survival pool pickers this week. There were two double-digit underdogs last week, but none this week. The highest spread on the board is the Cowboys -8.5 against a Buccaneers team that is having to start undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels due to Baker Mayfield's injury.

The question is: What's the Dolphins' spread and why isn't it higher? Miami has been at least a 9.5-point underdog three weeks in a row and will likely be a double-digit dog many other times this season. This week they host the Bengals and are 7- to 7.5-point underdogs to Cincinnati. The Dolphins failed to cover the spread in their first three games, but thanks to T.J. Hockenson at the end of last Sunday's game they did cover the spread in Week 4.

A T.J. Hockenson bad beat

In Week 4, we finally had a first crushing bad beat for bettors. But all Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson was doing was making a smart football play.

Vikings -11.5 bettors were finally going to get the result they wanted when Hockenson caught a pass near the end zone late in the game with the Vikings leading 15-10. He had a path to score. But instead of heading for the end zone and a touchdown, Hockenson slid down. He knew the Dolphins had no timeouts left and going down in bounds would essentially end the game.

Savvy play by TJ Hockenson to stop short of the end zone

MIAvsMIN on FOX/FOX One
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/z81tAE4wNy

— NFL (@NFL) October 4, 2026

The Vikings were able to kill the clock after that and won 15-10. Minnesota had plenty of other chances to score but settled for five field goals, and that's really what ruined Vikings bettors. But the final blow by Hockenson is what bettors will remember and lament.

item.title: Fantasy Football Backup RB Rankings for Week 5: RJ Harvey providing strong value in PPR formats
item.description: Fred Zinkie takes you through the top backup RBs for fantasy football going into Week 5.
item.content:encoded:
Fantasy football managers were reminded in Week 4 that astute waiver wire work can pay significant dividends. After all, those who grabbed Ollie Gordon II could have a long-term asset, while those who added Braelon Allen have a short-term solution for covering an injury at the position. The same may now be true of Emanuel Wilson, and Will Shipley is on the verge of becoming a hot commodity in fantasy circles. Here are the best backup RBs to roster right now.

Kyle Monangai, Bears (83% rostered on Yahoo)

After a game-changing Week 4 performance, Monangai is easily the best backup RB to roster right now. D’Andre Swift had a mediocre day on the ground (15-58) and did not receive a carry after a third-quarter fumble. Meanwhile, Monangai carried a Caleb Williams-less offense by gaining 146 yards on 30 carries and scoring twice.

Monangai now has more rushing yards and the same number of touchdowns as Swift. And while Williams is out of action, Monangai’s blend of physical running and explosiveness has made him arguably the most important member of the Bears offense. Swift remains the starter, but Monangai has advanced to the point where he is a desirable flex option.

Ollie Gordon II, Dolphins (62%)

Last week, I predicted that Gordon would get just one week in this column, as the Dolphins would immediately name him the starter in the absence of De’Von Achane. But the team threw us a curveball when they listed Jaylen Wright atop the depth chart, which gives me one more week to tout the value of Gordon. The second-year pro gained 100 yards on just nine carries against Minnesota in Week 4. Sure, his 53-yard run helped his final stat line, but Gordon still managed to gain 47 yards and a touchdown on his other eight rushes. As expected, he was a non-factor in the passing game.

The Dolphins offense may be the worst in the NFL, which significantly limits Gordon’s ceiling. But the punishing runner has better odds than anyone else on this list to lead his team in carries for the remainder of the season. With bye weeks beginning in Week 5, Gordon will be a useful RB2 or flex option at times over the next two months.

Emanuel Wilson, Seahawks (49%)

With Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet out, the door is wide open for Wilson to cement his role in Seattle’s offense. The former Packer took a big step in that direction in Week 4, when he scored twice and tallied 120 yards from scrimmage. George Holani, who was expected to have a significant role, totaled just 20 yards.

Charbonnet should return soon, and Price could be back by the end of October. In the meantime, Wilson is a viable RB2 in standard leagues. There is a chance that he plays well enough to stay ahead of Charbonnet, who could be rusty when he initially returns from surgery to repair a torn ACL. Although Seattle’s Monday addition of Joe Mixon sightly dampens the enthusiasm for Wilson, Mixon hasn’t played in an NFL game since 2024 and has plenty to prove before he becomes a factor.

RJ Harvey, Broncos (81%)

The Broncos’ offense continued to look sluggish on the ground in a Week 4 loss to the 49ers, with J.K. Dobbins and Harvey each averaging 3.6 yards per carry. But Harvey managed to make a significant impact in PPR leagues by producing 68 yards on 10 catches.

The good news for Harvey is that he leads the Broncos in catches (20). The bad news for the Broncos is that Harvey leads the team in catches. Denver will eventually get more production from its receivers, but it’s worth noting that it’s normal for a Sean Payton team to rank among the league leaders in catches by running backs. In standard formats, Harvey is a dud. But in PPR leagues, the second-year pro is a potential stud who is already a low-end RB2.

TreVeyon Henderson, Patriots (93%)

Although the Patriots will be proud of their statement win in Buffalo, the team’s running game was not a big part of the upset. Starter Rhamondre Stevenson gained 47 yards on 13 carries, while Henderson totaled 42 yards on 14 carries. Once again, Stevenson was used more prominently at the goal line and in the passing game.

Henderson will continue to have a role in the Patriots offense, but the second-year RB needs two things to happen in order to be more than a TD-dependent flex option. First, he needs the Patriots offense to get on track, which seemed to happen in Week 4. And second, he needs to get some involvement in the passing game, which doesn’t seem to be part of the game plan. Henderson remains a weak flex or RB2 option.

Rachaad White, Commanders (58%)

White didn’t miss much while resting a shoulder injury last week, as an injury to Marcus Mariota led to an ineffective Washington offense under third-string rookie Athan Kaliakmanis. Starter Jacory Croskey-Merritt (9 carries, 15 yards) struggled against a Colts defense that didn’t need to respect the passing game for most of the contest. Austin Ekeler (4 carries, 29 yards) made a small impact in White’s absence.

The good news for White and every other member of the Commanders offense is that Jayden Daniels could return for Week 5. White has some flex appeal with Daniels or Mariota under center, especially with Croskey-Merritt averaging 2.8 yards per carry this season.

Woody Marks, Texans (55%)

For the second straight week, it was Marks who found the end zone instead of starter David Montgomery. Marks also averaged 3.7 yards per carry in Week 4, which was better than the 2.4 average from Montgomery. Neither player was featured in the passing game, despite C.J. Stroud throwing for 347 yards in the loss to the Cowboys.

The Texans continue to struggle to run the ball, which is a problem that existed prior to 2026. Marks continues to get a handful of carries each week, and the door is wide open for the second-year pro to steal more opportunities from Montgomery. Unfortunately, neither player will be more than a TD-dependent flex option unless Stroud starts to direct more targets to his RBs.

Keaton Mitchell, Chargers (36%)

Although Mitchell didn’t gain ground on starter Omarion Hampton in Week 4, he continued to carve out a role in the offense. The speedster was respectable (39 yards) on 10 carries and also gained 24 yards on five catches. Hampton was slightly better on the ground but had minimal impact through the air.

The Chargers are 0-4 and in the next five weeks they will sandwich a bye week around games against strong defenses (Broncos, Chiefs, Rams, Texans). At best, Mitchell is a low-end flex option when managers deal with bye weeks.

Will Shipley, Eagles, (2%)

Saquon Barkley is dealing with a hamstring injury and Tank Bigsby (core muscle) is on his way to injured reserve, which means that Shipley is the only healthy RB on the Eagles active roster. The 24-year-old is hardly an exciting talent, having averaged 3.1 yards on 59 career carries. But the Eagles may have no choice but to give Shipley 10 carries and some passing-down work when they face the Jaguars this week in London. His ceiling would be low in a tough matchup, but the potential volume would make him a low-end flex option for at least one week.

Kaleb Johnson, Packers (6%)

Although Johnson hasn’t garnered much attention, he could be on the verge of claiming the RB1 role with the Packers. MarShawn Lloyd has done little with his opportunities, averaging 1.9 yards on seven carries in Week 4. Meanwhile, Johnson has shown some burst, especially he logged a 31-yard run in an eight-carry, 42-yard effort against the Bucs.

Lloyd caught five passes last week, and his skills in the passing game could keep him atop the depth chart. But the Packers’ running game has been a major problem this season, and one dominant game from Johnson could push him past Lloyd in terms of rushing volume. With the status of Josh Jacobs still up in the air, whoever grabs this job has the potential to keep it for the remainder of the season.

item.title: Cowboys rookie report: Quieter afternoon for the youngsters in Houston
item.description: Last week was a bit quiet for Cowboys rookies.
item.content:encoded:
Dallas secured a 34–30 victory over Houston on Sunday, climbing to 2–2 after CeeDee Lamb’s late touchdown. The comeback was largely led by the veterans, while the rookie class had a less impressive afternoon. Notably, none of Dallas’ rookie defenders recorded a sack, tackle for loss, interception, or pass defended. 

But here is how each rookie fared this week, listed in draft order, and any undrafted players worth noting after that. 

Caleb Downs

(55 defensive snaps | 7 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended)

Downs tied for the team lead in tackles, but Houston found success attacking his coverage. PFF charged him with five completions on five targets for 54 yards. Downs spent much more time as a coverage safety this week than in his normal ‘in the box’ alignment. The tackle production was welcome, preventing those catches is the next challenge. 

Malachi Lawrence

(20 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 1 pressure)

Lawrence produced one pressure on 10 pass-rush snaps. That provided a flash of disruption, although his overall contribution remained modest. Dallas needs its first-round edge defender to turn those rotational opportunities into more frequent problems for opposing quarterbacks, as this pass rush unit is starting looking very suspect. And being caught offside is never helpful for a defense that spent an afternoon finding ways to get Houston’s offense off the field. 

Jaishawn Barham

(39 defensive snaps | 1 tackle | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 1 pressure)

Barham generated a pressure on just two rushes, showing value when sent forward. Elsewhere, his impact was limited: PFF recorded a missed tackle against the run and a 13-yard completion on his only coverage target. This was one of the more quieter outings during a run of successful weeks Barham has been having. 

Drew Shelton

(1 offensive snap | 0 pressures allowed | 0 quarterback hits allowed | 0 sacks allowed)

Shelton’s lone offensive snap was a clean pass-blocking rep. That is a positive, but the workload offers little basis for a wider evaluation of his progress or readiness for a larger role. 

LT Overton

(20 defensive snaps | 2 tackles | 0 TFL | 0 sacks | 0 INT | 0 passes defended | 0 pressures)

Overton contributed two assisted tackles, but his 10 pass-rush snaps produced no pressure. He supplied rotation depth without delivering a disruptive play. More penetration would give Dallas a stronger return from this role, but the entire defensive line shows concern when it comes to generating consistent pressure in the pass rush.

item.title: Fantasy football waiver wire: 10 players to add for NFL Week 5
item.description: Several fantasy standouts have injury questions in Week 5. Are there any good pickups to fill the void? We have options as the bye weeks begin.
item.content:encoded:
Another week, another round of injuries in the NFL. (It never stops, does it?)

Perhaps the toughest part of seeing Lamar Jackson (ankle) or Ja'Marr Chase (concussion) go down is not knowing how badly they're hurt. Both players exited Sunday's games early and didn't return. Their status for this week's game is unlikely to be determined by the time fantasy league waivers run.

Even if you don't have Jackson or Chase on your roster, there's still the specter of the bye week rearing its ugly head. Week 5 begins the run of two or more NFL teams not playing, with the Carolina Panthers and Kansas City Chiefs getting the week off.

Fantasy football players to add for Week 5

Due to the wide variance in types of leagues and individual team needs, the players listed here include their availability rates in Yahoo leagues, which may or may not match rates on other platforms. (Suggested bid values based on $100 free agent acquisition budget for the season.)

For customized waiver wire suggestions, synced to your league, subscribe to USA TODAY Sports Fantasy's exclusive tools.

RB Emanuel Wilson, Seattle Seahawks (49% rostered)

Rookie Jadarian Price was unexpectedly put on injured reserve last week due to a chest injury, leaving Wilson as the top running back on the depth chart. He responded with an excellent outing against the Chargers, racking up 81 rushing yards and a TD on 21 carries and catching three passes for 39 more yards. Zack Charbonnet (knee) isn't quite ready to come off the PUP list, so it's Wilson's job for another week against the 49ers (Recommended FAAB bid: $11)

RB Tyler Allgeier, Arizona Cardinals (37% rostered)

Rookie Jeremiyah Love's surprising admission that the coaching staff is managing his workload may not sit well with fantasy managers. His persistent ankle issues may also be playing a role in Allgeier getting more snaps. Regardless, the numbers don't lie. Allgeier looked good against the Giants on his eight carries for 42 yards, 22 of them coming on a first-quarter TD burst. (FAAB bid: $9)

WR Dohnte Meyers, Cincinnati Bengals (1% rostered)

Chase still needs to clear the NFL's concussion protocol in order to play this week against the Dolphins. In addition, No. 2 wideout Tee Higgins also left Sunday's game early with an injury. That left Meyers as the top pass-catching option for QB Joe Burrow. The former CFL standout hauled in seven of his nine targets for 82 yards and will likely have a major role again on Sunday. (FAAB bid: $8)

WR Keon Coleman, Buffalo Bills (5% rostered)

Coleman has been an enigma throughout his three NFL seasons. But after top receiver DJ Moore left Sunday's game with a shoulder injury, Coleman rose to the occasion. He caught six passes for 116 yards and a touchdown, producing the biggest fantasy game of his career. Do we dare believe he's turned a corner? (Or a safety? Or a linebacker?) (FAAB bid: $7)

RBs Will Shipley/Dameon Pierce, Philadelphia Eagles (2% rostered)

Saquon Barkley exited Sunday's game early with a hamstring injury and is week-to-week. Backup Tank Bigsby suffered an abdominal injury that landed him on IR. That leaves Shipley has the only healthy running back on the active roster. The Eagles will certainly add a couple players off the practice squad for Sunday's game at Jacksonville (Dameon Pierce, Jaydon Blue and Carson Steele are possibilities), but Shipley will likely garner most of the touches. (FAAB bid: $6. Backup bid: $2 on Pierce)

WR Darius Cooper, Philadelphia Eagles (0% rostered)

The Eagles were also without top receiver DeVonta Smith against the Rams. While the passing game continues to struggle overall, QB Jalen Hurts did connect with Cooper for a pair of touchdowns. He only caught three of seven targets overall for 33 yards, but the red zone looks are enough to warrant a modest bid, especially for fantasy managers who have Smith. (FAAB bid: $4)

WR Efton Chism III, New England Patriots (0% rostered)

Coach Mike Vrabel admitted he needs to find more playing time for Chism after he hauled in what proved to be the game-winning TD pass against Buffalo with under two minutes remaining in the fourth quarter. That was one of only two receptions on the day for 42 yards. We'll see if Vrabel can be taken at his word. It's already a pretty crowded receiving room as it is in New England. (FAAB bid: $2)

QB Jacoby Brissett, Arizona Cardinals (16% rostered)

Perhaps the best widely available quarterback this week, Brissett has an enticing matchup against the NFL's worst pass defense, the Detroit Lions. He only threw for 166 yards in a Week 4 loss to the Giants, but he did have a pair of TD passes. The three interceptions, on the other hand, were a problem. Consider him a bye-week stopgap. (FAAB bid: $2)

QB Tyler Huntley, Baltimore Ravens (0% rostered)

If you have Jackson and his status remains unclear by the time waiver pickups are due, Huntley may be your best option. The Ravens play on Sunday night at Atlanta, so unless you're able to pivot to Michael Penix Jr., having Huntley and Jackson will give you the freedom to make a game-time decision if needed. (FAAB bid: $1)

item.title: Colts DE Arden Key to miss time with hamstring injury
item.description: The Colts won't have defensive end Arden Key in the lineup for a while.
item.content:encoded:
The Colts won't have defensive end Arden Key in the lineup for a while.

Key injured his hamstring in Sunday's 30-13 win over the Commanders in London and head coach Shane Steichen said at a Monday press conference that Key is going to miss more time moving forward. Jeremy Fowler of ESPN reports that Key is expected to miss three or four weeks.

That timeline could make Key a candidate for injured reserve, which would mean he'd miss at least four games. The Colts play the Steelers, Titans, Vikings and Jaguars in the next four weeks.

Key has eight tackles, a half-sack and a forced fumble so far this season.

item.title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL, Week 4: Bears QB musical chairs wins again
item.description: On @kdthompson5’s 10 Thoughts on the NFL: the running backs are back, refs are out of control, Chargers, Bills, Cowboys, Bears and more!
item.content:encoded:
1. At first, I admit I found myself getting irritated at fans wondering if Ben Johnson could win with Justin Fields and Mitchell Trubisky after what he’s done in back-to-back weeks with Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent in Chicago Bears wins. On second thought, though: screw it. So I’m asking you all: would Johnson get a win with: A. Fields, B. Trubisky, C. both, or D. neither against the Green Bay Packers in Week 4? Given the state of that team, I’m tempted to go with C. But in practical terms—as much as it pains me—I’m going B. Fields never beat the Packers when he was here. Trubisky did. And even though Fields is way more talented and explosive, Trubisky is the more likely to just do what Johnson says and get it over with. (I’d take Trubisky over Bagent, personally.)

2. I already have a major problem with fans getting too personal with athletes at sporting events. (Just because you paid for a seat does not mean you have carte blanche to be an idiot.) But what is with these officials lately? Now, on one hand, I get the refs needing to maintain some boundaries, because players can’t be just saying and doing anything to officials out there. But we didn’t come here to watch refs cuss out the players over incidental contact or disagreeing with calls. This ain’t the ‘80s and ‘90s NBA!

3. I hate that injury for Tyquan Thornton, a guy I covered when I was in New England. The former second-round pick was four games into the best season he’s ever had as a pro and was going off on the Las Vegas Raiders when he dislocated his ankle late in the game. Now, his season is probably just about over. Some will think mainly about the excitement of the Kansas City Chiefs possibly bringing back Tyreek Hill to fill the void. But here’s hoping Thornton makes a recovery as fast as he is. You hate to see guys like that, whom Patrick Mahomes called “one of the best teammates he’s ever had,” go down.

4. The running back is BACK, baby. Especially if you play for the Atlanta Falcons and your name is B. Robinson, apparently. Between the two running backs named B. Robinson in their backfield (Bijan and Brian), the Falcons got a video game-like 207 rushing yards and five touchdowns, including a 59-yard scamper from Bijan that made the Saints defense look like it was moving in slow motion. Whichever B. Robinson you got for your fantasy team, congratulations. You really ate with that.

5. I just want to point out that some people I know balked at the idea of Tetairoa McMillan, who just put up 192 yards and two TDs on Sunday Night Football against the Detroit Lions, being a better NFL prospect in the 2025 NFL Draft than Rome Odunze was in 2024. Not that this has any bearing on the Bears, of course. (Still plenty happy with the Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III picks, thanks very much.) It’s just a reminder that: 1. everyone makes mistakes, and 2. sometimes, it’s best not to overthink it. Ballers ball.

6. I’m going to ignore the fact that my praying on Deshaun Watson’s downfall in Cleveland isn’t going very well—damn you, Todd Monken—and shout out the hilarity of Mike McCarthy’s and Aaron Rodgers’ second marriage breaking down in public on Thursday Night Football. McCarthy mouthing “f— a—“ under his breath after Rodgers (kind of rightfully) screams at him to call a play before the play clock winds down is all of us. 

7. Last year, the Patriots used their first game against the Buffalo Bills in Orchard Park as a statement game to the rest of the NFL en route to making a Super Bowl. This year, it was a get-right game for an offense that hasn’t done much right. The real Drake Maye finally re-emerged (269 yards passing, three TDs) and redeemed himself in the clutch, throwing a touchdown to Efton Chism (who made an insane grab, by the way) in about the same spot he tossed his game-losing pick against Seattle in Week 1. The vibes still aren’t quite right with this squad. With that being said, though, they’re still right in the mix at 2-2. You’ll take that, all things considered.

8. It might’ve just been one highlight against a guy who doesn’t tackle for a living, but Lord did Jacksonville cornerback Travis Hunter snatch Cincinnati’s Tee Higgins’ ankles on that interception return. Might’ve taken his soul right along with it. That move alone is why he still gets offensive snaps despite playing full-time as a cornerback these days. Don’t be surprised when he gets a touch next week after that highlight makes the rounds.

9. Sometimes, you just have to call it what it is: Justin Herbert stinks right now. Maybe it’s just growing pains under Mike McDaniel. Maybe it’s the inevitable Jim Harbaugh clock running its course—he’s never lasted more than four seasons anywhere as a head coach in the NFL. Or maybe he was always closer to this level of breakdown than we thought. But, in short, this is why it hurts so much when you pay the wrong guy. Because this version of Herbert is simply not getting you anywhere but last place in the division and fired.

10. Let’s just be real clear about this: the backlash to Carlie Gordon-Irsay being on the sidelines of Colts games and trying to learn about the team she owns is dumb. Really dumb. And it’s even worse listening to really dumb people talk about it. I mean…if you were going to run a billion-dollar business (which almost none of us will), you don’t think you’d want to learn as much as possible about how that business works as you can and why people do the things they do? And to those who say, “Not even Jerry Jones would do that!”—you know what Jerry Jones would do? Hire Brian Schottenheimer because football runs in his blood, or whatever. Bears fans complain about the McCaskeys not understanding football and not knowing how to fire football people all the time. Now, you have an owner—a woman, at that, which makes the trolls even more rabid—who actually gives enough of a damn to do things a different way, and it’s weird? Okay. Y’all got it. Guess we like our owners stupid then. Good to know.

item.title: 5 cool things the Seahawks did in Chargers win that they haven’t done in years
item.description: Hey, let’s focus on some good things the Seahawks did in a win, not just the preponderance of penalties!
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks may not have played their cleanest football (to put it kindly) against the Los Angeles Chargers, but they still won the game and had some cool moments along the way. Not everything has to be focused on the penalties or the dueling interceptions to start a game, not when the Seahawks did some good things we haven’t seen from them in a good while!

The first Seahawks running back screen pass touchdown in six years

Their first touchdown came on a screen pass—yes, a “screen pass”—to Emanuel Wilson, who recorded his first Seahawks TD on a 23-yard scamper. It’s only the second receiving touchdown of Wilson’s NFL career.

The Seahawks passing game is not known for featuring running backs as receivers. Brian Fleury was supposed to get the backs more involved as passing targets, and so far there’s been at least some semblance of an effort even if it’s not in high volume. It’s a running joke among Seahawks fans that the team is/has been notoriously bad at screen passes, particularly to the backs, such that the Wilson TD felt like something from a parallel universe.

What’s the last Seahawks screen pass touchdown to a running back? You have to go back to the cavernous feeling of the 2020 pandemic season, when fans were either not allowed in the stands or there in limited capacity. Chris Carson’s second receiving touchdown of the quarter from Russell Wilson couldn’t have been much easier. You can even hear Atlanta Falcons defenders and coaches yelling “SCREEN!” as they hopelessly chase a lost cause.

Ernest Jones IV pulls a Bobby Wagner daily double

Seattle’s elite middle linebacker destroyed the Chargers offense. Whether it was stopping the run, getting after Justin Herbert, defending receivers in the pass game, or creating turnovers, Jones might end up with an NFC Defensive Player of the Week award come Wednesday.

Jones picked up his first sack of the season on a blitz that the Chargers had seven in protection for and didn’t come remotely close to stopping.

The next possession was Jones’ first interception of the year, one that might as well have been catching practice given Herbert threw the ball directly in his lane.

Jones became the first Seahawks linebacker since Bobby Wagner to record a sack and an interception in the same game. Wagner did it in 2018 against the San Francisco 49ers, sacking Nick Mullens before setting a franchise record with a 98-yard interception return for a touchdown. Bobby also had a sack and a pick against the Minnesota Vikings in 2013.

Seahawks score 30+ points in three straight games for first time since 2020

Ahhh the Let Russ Cook year. Might have been a blessing in disguise given what soon transpired out of that season. Seattle started the year scoring 38, 35, 38, and 31 points out of the gate, starting the season 4-0. They also put up 34, 37, and 34 points later in the season, but lost two of those games and so went the LRC movement.

It might not feel like it, but the Seahawks have scored 92 points (31, 31, and 30) over the past three weeks. The offense hasn’t been at its sharpest but they are scoring.

Rashid Shaheed is the first Seahawks receiver to get a rushing TD since…

Shaheed finally got his first offensive touchdown in a Seahawks uniform. No, it wasn’t on a catch, but he impacted the run game with a couple of carries for 33 yards. His 28-yard touchdown run is Seattle’s longest rush of the season.

A Seahawks receiver scoring a touchdown isn’t something that we have seen a lot more recently than the other facts. You just probably don’t remember that the previous WR rushing touchdown was scored by… JAKE BOBO! Yes, Bobo received a handoff near the goal line and scored against the Cleveland Browns back in 2023.

Before Bobo, the last Seahawks rushing touchdown by a receiver was Tyler Lockett’s 75-yard jet sweep score in the 2016 win over the Carolina Panthers.

Drake Thomas’ first play pick

Justin Herbert clearly loves him some Seahawks linebackers, because before Ernest got his INT, Drake Thomas snagged Herbert’s first throw of the game.

Yes, we know the Seahawks wasted this with an immediate interception at the other end, but this was an excellent start for the defense after not forcing any takeaways last week. It’s the first time the Seahawks have recorded a first play INT since supreme ball-hawk Quandre Diggs got Derek Carr in a 2022 loss to the Las Vegas Raiders. Maybe it’s an AFC West thing.

So while it’s easy to be steamed at the very real issues we saw in the Chargers game, Seattle still produced some significant performances and highlights worth praising. They’re still 3-1, they’re still the reigning Super Bowl champions, and you know Mike Macdonald and that locker room will not be complacent with “a win is a win” mentality.

OK, my ears must hear different things than the broadcasters who say, “Look at what Jeff Hafley is building. Just wait until he gets the players!”  They didn’t say, “Let’s aspire to be the Green Bay Packers! The ACME of NFL franchises.” I have a question: be TOTALLY honest and don’t cheat! What does the word ACME actually mean? Don’t cheat! Be honest with your answers, which will make things funnier in the comments! To end my digression: go see Coyote vs Acme!!!!

The New Packers???

Back to aspiring to be the Green Bay Packers! What the hell has the Green Bay Packers organization done since winning the Super Bowl with Aaron Rodgers in 2011? Yes, 2011!  Is that what we want to aspire to? Really, we were whipping their asses when Tua injured his noggin for the 8th time. I don’t get it. Maybe I don’t understand the goal? Would you rather be the NY Giants and win 2 Super Bowls with Eli but suffer 11 years of mediocrity in return, or be the KC Chiefs under Schottenheimer and go 11-5 every year but never even SNIFF the Super Bowl? The Phins were once like that too, and the stadium in the 80s used to flash these graphics showing the Phins were the most successful sports franchise ever! Highest winning percentage! Ha! Those were the days. And don’t forget we lost 2 AFC Championships at home under Marino. But with #13 we were never out of the game. And that, right there, keeps me faithful. I keep hearing that the GB cap situation is good, blah blah blah. What does that have to do with winning Super Bowls?

Phincidents!

I am watching what the Saints did with Drew Brees and Sean Payton. It eats me alive; I must admit. I also remember a classic episode of South Park in 2004 where Cartman dons a cardboard box pretending to be a robot called Awesome-O. During the episode, Awesome-O is asked: “Who’s gonna win the Super Bowl?” Awesome-O answers, “The New Orleans Saints,” to mocking laughter from the crowd and me at the time. Guess what? Awesome-O was correct, just like the Coyote during his trial!

Devon Godchaux (Miami Dolphins 5th round pick 2017) is still playing for the Saints! Wow! God Bless Him! Laissez les bon temps rouler! And the halftime show! Wowwie wow Wow! says the Continental! Was he Cajun?

Back to this coaching staff: I have heard some strange statements like “Miami has trouble covering TEs.” This is untrue and gives too much credit to the Phins. The statement should be “Miami has never heard of the TE position and doesn’t believe that it exists.” I have never watched a game or heard of a game where the TE was targeted 14 times(whatever) and every target was caught (until Sunday). Is this what Coach Hafley is bringing to the Phins? This is a pure unadulterated embarrassment. On the last 3rd down play, I was screaming, “Don’t fall for the brush block and drift garbage that was taught to me in 1974.” I thought the great Green Bay standard bearer Jeff Hafley would have done SOMETHING to slow down this average TE. He isn’t Gronk, Jason Witten, Tony Gonzalez, or even Russ Francis (look him up). Where is the “secret sauce” that Hafley is bringing; where are the stratagems! I have played in hundreds of pick-up games where I would “bird dog” that play and bait the QB into throwing that pass. But my God, he would have scored in a “tag” game. How can we take this organization seriously when they don’t know what a TE is? Do they cover TEs in Green Bay? Is that something they teach in year two of the rebuild? Do they play special teams in Green Bay? The word is out on the street: the Phins special teams play is hot garbage, and there are opportunities to exploit. The TE position on the opposing team is the Road Runner, and we’re never gonna catch him.

item.title: Rams Film Room: Kyren Williams is a weapon as a receiver
item.description: The running back played a huge role in the Rams’ win over the Eagles
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Rams needed Kyren Williams to come up big in Week 4, and the veteran running back did just that.

In a win over the Philadelphia Eagles that was anything but pretty for the Rams offense, Williams became a vital outlet for the passing game while also being his typically efficient self on the ground. This was especially important in a game where Los Angeles’s second-best pass catcher, Davante Adams, struggled uncharacteristically and frustratingly.

Williams caught a career-high 10 passes against the Eagles, six of which were “successful” (based on generally accepted calculations for success rate), while three turned into new first downs for the Rams (another would have led to a manageable 4th-and-1 situation but was aided by a penalty on the Eagles).

We’re going to look at one play in particular from this week’s fourth-quarter comeback, in which Sean McVay and L.A. weaponized Williams against an ill-equipped Philadelphia linebackers group.

And the end zone view:

The Rams will always be happy with Kyren Williams matched up one-on-one in space against Jihaad Campbell (11). These choice routes are a staple of McVay’s offense and in this situation it sets up a scoring opportunity moments later.

Williams is even with Campbell after releasing from the backfield with a gaping hole in the middle of the field. The veteran running back takes the inside option, running the angle route across quarterback Matthew Stafford’s face and beating Campbell to the spot. The linebacker didn’t gain any depth here, leaving him no margin for error before the running back breaks inward. He’s dropped at the one-yard line but punched it in to cap the 98-yard scoring drive.

HB Angle on the goal line is always a good call, but when you’ve got a linebacker on skates from the start you’re in excellent shape. McVay and all the coaches from his tree (Kyle Shanahan and his coaching descendants included) thrive on putting linebackers in conflict. Again, the Rams are going to attack Campbell or a similar player every single time in this spot.

If this concept looks at least vaguely familiar, it should. It led to a Williams touchdown reception in Week 2 against the New York Giants.

The setup here is very similar to this week’s case study. The Rams are in 11 personnel both times, the only difference being the tight end is aligned to the right of the formation in Week 4 instead of the left like he is in Week 2. It’s out and up out of the backfield for Williams, once again putting a linebacker, in this case rookie Arvell Reese, in conflict.

That’s where we start to see some differences. Here, Reese does gain depth and also has help in between the hashes, putting a lid on the potential for Williams should he take the inbreaking option. That depth, however, opens a huge passing lane for Stafford as his running back takes the vertical option instead. Reese and co. took away the angle, but Williams still split him and the boundary defender with a seam route for a 10-yard touchdown snag.

The great Dan Casey broke down this particular play on Twitter as part of a longer deep dive on the Rams, which is worth your time.

McVay and the Rams offense have a great deal of trust in Williams, and it allows them to pick defenses apart in the low red zone. You can’t do this with every running back, but with one with good hands and a legitimate route tree it opens up so many potentially explosive opportunities.

Los Angeles needed someone to step up on offense to beat the Eagles this week, and Williams, paired with an old faithful option from the playbook, answered the call.

item.title: What do the Packers do without linebacker Edgerrin Cooper?
item.description: Losing Edgerrin Cooper raises another frustrating question for the Packers: how do you live without him?
item.content:encoded:
How do you replace Edgerrin Cooper?

You don’t.

There, the intro for this edition of our Tuesday links column is done! We’ve solved the Packers’ post-Cooper linebacker dilemma by identifying that there is no solution.

But seriously, I’m always a little frustrated (annoyed? vexed?) by the intractable situation that arises whenever the Packers lose a key player. It’s both impossible to come up with a solution, because certain players certainly approach irreplaceability, and an essential question, because you’re not going to just play with 10 players on the field because one guy suddenly finds himself short an Achilles tendon.

You’re clearly never going to find a one-to-one replacement for Edgerrin Cooper. His stat line from Sunday (nine tackles, a sack, and an interception) has only been produced by a Packers player three other times this century (by Xavier McKinney in 2025, Charles Woodson in 2009, and Nate Wayne in 2001). Players like Edgerrin Cooper don’t grow on trees, and the truly annoying part is that he appeared to only be getting better.

But you need a solution. What’s it going to be? It’s not leaning more heavily on Zaire Franklin; his workload is big enough already and his limitations as an undersized linebacker on the wrong side of 30 are apparent. It’s not turning to Isaiah McDuffie; we’ve seen that movie before. It’s not Ty’Ron Hopper; if he were any good, we’d have seen it by now.

So what’s it going to be? How do you keep getting plays from your defense while offsetting the loss of one of your very best players?

Throw it on the pile, because this is just another question that will define the Packers’ season. There may not be a satisfying answer, but the Packers are obligated to try to find one.

Probably understating it a bit.

item.title: 5 final observations from the 49ers win over the Broncos
item.description: What stood out from the 49ers win on Sunday?
item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco 49ers used a fourth-quarter touchdown from George Kittle to beat the Denver Broncos 24-14 on Sunday night, getting past another marquee opponent as they climbed to 4-0.

This game was a different type of win for the 49ers, as the offense didn’t hum at its usual level, while the defense mitigated the damage until things popped up for San Francisco in the fourth quarter.

Nonetheless, they got a big victory, and now lead to Lumen Field for their third divisional game of the season. Before that, let’s take a look back at the Broncos game and talk through some observations.

1. Brock Purdy looks like an MVP candidate

For the first time in his NFL career, Brock Purdy has been receiving a ton of national praise this season, as he’s jumped into the MVP mix as a legitimate contender.

So far, Purdy has thrown for 1,007 yards, 11 touchdowns, and one interception, while his 89.7 QBR ranks first in the NFL. One thing I’ve noticed that was previously a problem for Purdy is that he’s not bailing clean pockets nearly as much anymore. He has more trust in his offensive line, and that’s given him more time to process through reads and hit his progressions.

Purdy also just looks poised out there. He doesn’t seem flustered, and that’s what makes him look like an NFL quarterback. I know development isn’t a big word out in the NFL as much anymore, but I really think we’ve seen Purdy continue to grow as a quarterback in a big way in Year 5.

2. Raheem Morris is a special coordinator

Man, Raheem Morris called a heck of a game. The 49ers entered this one badly injured along the defensive line. They were facing what many presumed to be an elite offensive line, and yet, San Francisco regularly won the line of scrimmage in the run game.

Morris’s ability to create pressure situations on Bo Nix on Sunday was great. Corners are playing aggressively under him, and that happened again on Sunday. The linebackers flow freely. There is clear defensive alignment on the field with what Morris wants to do.

I’ve been impressed by how Morris has kept certain factors similar in San Francisco, but also proven why he’s an elite defensive coordinator with his own sprinkles.

3. The Niners need a WR

While Brock Purdy trusted his offensive line, it’s clear that didn’t apply to his receivers. And rightfully so, given their struggles on Sunday.

Jacob Cowing and Jordan Watkins combined for 46 snaps, with a lot of them coming out wide. They were both complete non-factors, and we saw several times when Purdy was a little more hesitant than usual to rip it, instead checking it down.

Brandin Cooks also had a rough stretch of plays, and looked like someone still grasping the playbook. Mike Evans is clearly lingering, and the 49ers are stretched thin at receiver. That feels like the one thing that could hold this offense back.

5. Kyle Shanahan calls another good end to the game

I continue to like Kyle Shanahan’s aggressiveness to end games, as the 49ers didn’t capitulate after the Broncos cut it to within three on Sunday.

I thought Shanahan could’ve definitely been more aggressive with the passing game in the first half, but with the heat and his receiver play, it made sense why the game played out the way it did early for the 49ers.

But the 49ers found their way to explosives, both thanks to Purdy’s doing and an aggressive outlook from Shanahan to cap the game. He’s had another excellent start to the season as a play-caller.

item.description: NFL trade rumors start to swirl, should the Cleveland Browns acquire DE Khalil Mack? His contract, performance say yes
item.content:encoded:
With the Cleveland Browns 3-1 and at the top of the AFC North heading into Week 5 as underdogs on the road against the New York Jets, everything around the team is more fun. Talk of trading away a wide receiver or quarterback is about what is best for the team, not just about adding draft capital for the future.

With the NFL trade deadline over a month away, the Browns have five games to make a decision about what direction they see the team going after the deadline. That doesn’t mean GM Andrew Berry will wait. DE Khalil Mack is already rumored to be on the market and fits a role that Cleveland could use help with: pass rush.

Berry spent most of the offseason trying to add another edge player, and that was before DE Alex Wright was lost for the season due to injury. The 35-year-old Mack, who signed a one-year deal to return to the Los Angeles Chargers, may be the first big domino to fall as his team has floundered to a 0-4 start.

Mack’s $18 million contract seems big, but a trade would only cost the Browns a portion of the $8 million in base salary, as the Chargers paid $10 million as a signing bonus. As Jack Duffin of The OBR explains, how much it would cost Cleveland depends on when a deal happened:

Quick math says that acquiring Mack this week would cost just over $6 million in cap space and that would drop about a million every two weeks. At the start of the season, Berry had over $12 million in cap space to work with and could get creative with Mack’s contract if the two sides were amenable.

Is Mack’s performance at age 35 worth it?

So far, the veteran has three sacks, five QB hits, and five tackles for loss in four contests. Pro Football Focus has him ranked 13th in total pressures in the NFL and gave him an 86.1 grade in Week 4:

Mack produced one sack and four pressures while leading the team with four stops. He also posted an 82.0 in run defense and a 69.6 in pass rush (second best on the team).

Suffice to say, Mack continues to produce.

Given his age, production, and salary, Los Angeles is likely to receive a high Day 3 pick for the veteran pass rusher. It is also possible, especially for a team like the Browns with a lot of young players, that the Chargers attempt to do a player-for-player swap instead of draft capital.

Are you in favor of the Browns trading for Mack? If so, how high of a draft pick would you be willing to give up? If not, who do you think the team should be looking to add in a trade?

item.title: Lions center Cade Mays likely to return to practice this week
item.description: The Detroit Lions could get some more help on offense with the return of center Cade Mays.
item.content:encoded:
The Detroit Lions are continuing to get some positive injury news. After telling local media on Monday that they hope to get Pro Bowl safety Brian Branch back to practice this week, Lions coach Dan Campbell told 97.1 The Ticket on Tuesday that starting center Cade Mays is also expected to return to practice this week.

“He’s doing great,” Campbell said. “He and Branch are on the same plan right now. So the plan is to get them worked into practice. We’re waiting on the final call from the doctor on both to say, ‘Yes, they can practice.’ We’d love to get them going this week. Doesn’t mean they’re going to play (vs. Cardinals).”

Mays suffered a wrist fracture early in training camp, after the Lions gave him a three-year, $25 million contract to fill their void at center—still vacant by the retirement of Frank Ragnow last year and the cost-cutting release of Graham Glasgow earlier this season.

As Campbell alluded to, just because Mays and Branch are returning to practice doesn’t mean they will play in this Sunday’s game against the Cardinals. Their return to practice opens a 21-day evaluation period where the Lions can activate each player from their injury list ot the 53-man roster at any time. But until that happens, they won’t count against the roster. Typically, the Lions have preferred to give players coming off a long-term injury at least two weeks of practice before activating them.

Mays’ return would be a help to an offensive line that has played well, but inconsistently. Detroit has allowed just eight sacks through four games, but their 4.2 yards per carry on the ground rank just 16th in the NFL.

In Mays’ absence, Juice Scruggs has played valiantly, but the center job almost certainly belongs to Mays when he’s ready to go. That said, last week Campbell noted that Scruggs would be considered in the left guard competition upon Mays’ return.

item.title: AP NFL Power Rankings Week 5: Top 5 gets shaken up
item.description: The Arrowhead Pride team ranks the league from top to bottom.
item.content:encoded:
And just like that, a quarter of the NFL season is behind us. Three unbeatens remain, all with warts but all continuing to win at the end of the day. The NFL continues to surprise us on a weekly basis, as it truly is an any-given-Sunday type of league.

You would have been called crazy if you told us the following in August:

  • The Las Vegas Raiders’ resurgence with 38-year-old quarterback Kirk Cousins playing the best football of his life. The Raiders appear to be the second-best team in the AFC West.
  • A Kansas City Chiefs running back in an Andy Reid offense leads the NFL in rushing and is on pace for well over 2,000 yards.
  • The San Francisco 49ers appear to be the dream team, unlike their NFC West rivals, the Los Angeles Rams.
  • The Los Angeles Chargers are unwatchable, and if this continues, they could face major decisions in the 2027 offseason at quarterback.
  • The Minnesota Vikings are undefeated, yet field one of the NFL’s most horrific offenses.

And that’s just a few examples. We love the NFL for its unpredictability, and it keeps delivering week after week.

How predictable or unpredictable was the Arrowhead Pride staff this week? Read on to find out.

Biggest riser: Carolina Panthers +6

Biggest faller: Pittsburgh Steelers -6 (In our Week 4 Power Rankings, the Steelers were tied for the biggest riser)

This week, along with myself, staff voters were: Maurice Elston, Caleb James, Ron Kopp Jr., Rocky Magana, Jared Sapp, and Matt Stagner.

1. San Francisco 49ers (1st)

I want to see studies run on that electric substation. Another star, fullback Kyle Jusczyk will miss time with an injury. Yet this team keeps winning.

Tyquan Thornton, please take my ankle. I don’t need it.

3. Jacksonville Jaguars (4th)

The London fans will not recognize their hometown Jaguars in the next two weeks. This is a complete football team.

4. Seattle Seahawks (5th)

How much regret is there for paying Rashid Shaheed over Kenneth Walker III?

5. Buffalo Bills (2nd)

I was once told that Josh Allen was the greatest decision-maker with the football in the NFL. After throwing a game-ending interception and losing at home to the hapless Patriots, I was again told that Josh Allen was the greatest decision-maker with the football in the NFL.

6. Baltimore Ravens (6th)

This team drops big time in the rankings if Lamar Jackson misses time with an injury.

7. Minnesota Vikings (9th)

Their offense is within the ranks of the powerhouses known as the Titans’ and Dolphins’ offenses in yards per game. Ugly, yet they remain undefeated.

The Rams are relying on Sean McVay pep talks to muster comebacks. The offseason champs have simply looked unimpressive to start the season.

9. Chicago Bears (11th)

The Bears have looked better with Caleb Williams on the sideline…

10. Cincinnati Bengals (7th)

Personally, I’m a major fan of the Bengals’ undying loyalty to head coaches.

11. Philadelphia Eagles (8th)

This team needs a hard reset.

12. Las Vegas Raiders (12th)

Andy Reid is now the winningest head coach at Allegiant Stadium Arrowhead West.

13. Denver Broncos (14th)

Denver can’t run the football, and Jaylen Waddle has been virtually non-existent in this offense. How long will Sean Payton sit idly by and let Davis Webb run this offense?

14. Dallas Cowboys (15th)

What I’d give for Patrick Mahomes to have a wide receiver weapon like CeeDee Lamb…

The championship window is gone.

16. New England Patriots (20th)

We’ll find out soon enough if this performance says more about Drake Maye or the Bills’ putrid defense.

17. New York Giants (19th)

The Jameis Winston experience is fully here.

18. Cleveland Browns (22nd)

This is exactly the type of underdog team Americans would love to get behind. Except for one major elephant in the room.

19. Indianapolis Colts (17th)

I wonder what Colts’ owner Carlie Irsary-Gordon is asking assistant coaches and sideline personnel during game action. She’s making Jerry Jones look hands-off.

20. Carolina Panthers (26th)

They’re building something special in Carolina. Bryce Young continues to prove the doubters wrong.

21. New Orleans Saints (18th)

Very anticlimactic performance in the Katrina anniversary game.

22. Pittsburgh Steelers (16th)

Watching the old married couple Rodgers and McCarthy curse and fight on primetime television is objectively hilarious.

23. Atlanta Falcons (25th)

I did not see this complete turnaround coming with the return of Michael Penix Jr.

24. Arizona Cardinals (21st)

I once again ask, what do the Cardinals want for Marvin Harrison Jr.? Get on the phone over the bye week, Mr. Veach.

The Texans played a reverse card to start the season. CJ Stroud is playing well enough to win football games, but this defense looks lost. The Texans played a reverse card to start the season. CJ Stroud is playing well enough to win football games, but this defense looks lost.

26. Green Bay Packers (23rd)

An uninspiring performance with a three-point victory over a winless team, starting a rookie quarterback in their first start. Not sure anyone’s jobs were saved in this one.

I’d be very nervous to see Jaylen Daniels back on the field so soon if I were a Commanders fan. It’s just not possible for that elbow to be fully right.
