item.title: Pro Football Focus grades and advanced stats for the Giants’ victory over the Cardinals
item.description: An uneven performance, but several players are making their presence felt
item.content:encoded:
The New York Giants have only played one game against an elite team this season, and that was a resounding loss, so we shouldn’t conclude too much at this early stage. With all due respect to Bill Parcells, you may not always be what your record says you are. Still, you have to take care of business against opponents as they come up on the schedule, and with one exception, the Giants have done that well and find themselves sitting in first place in the NFC East. Will they continue to grow, as their predecessors in the 1984 and 2005 seasons did on their way to eventual Super Bowls several years later? We don’t know, but looking at the performances of individual players is one way to see whether hope for the future is justified. Let’s look at Pro Football Focus grades and other advanced stats to learn about who played well and who didn’t. Elite players are beginning to emerge on both sides of the ball for this team.

PFF grades: Offense

We finally saw something like the 2024 version of Malik Nabers on Sunday. Nabers was targeted seven times and caught six for 112 yards and his first touchdown of the year. That’s 18.7 yards per reception. Three of his catches were explosive plays, just what the Giants offense has been needing this season:

That performance earned him an overall outstanding 89.2 grade.

The other Giants receivers all made contributions as well, with Theo Johnson making only his second catch of the season a beauty on a thread-the-needle throw from Winston, Isaiah Likely bringing down another 7 (22 on the season), and rookie Malachi Fields catching his weekly two balls (he’s had two every week so far), one of them for his first NFL touchdown.

The running backs had a workmanlike rather than impressive performance, although 43 of Cam Skattebo’s 58 yards were after contact, which seems to be the norm for him. The one blemish was Najee Harris’ fumble.

The offensive line was a mixed bag. We are seeing the cumulative effect of Andrew Thomas’ groin, knee, and ankle injuries. He’s playing through it all, but so far he’s not the player we’ve become used to. Thomas hasn’t given up a sack yet (though he had some responsibility for Jaxson Dart’s knee injury in the Rams game), but he’s allowed eight pressures already, three against Arizona. On the right side, however, Jermaine Eluemunor is off to a great start, with only one hurry yesterday (in addition to a penalty) and only three pressures (one sack) total for the season. Jon Runyan Jr. gave up a sack an two hurries yesterday, but overall his pass blocking has been solid and his run blocking his improved since the first two games. Sisi Mauigoa, on the other hand, is having some “welcome to the NFL” moments. Sunday he surrendered five pressures including one sack, his worst game to date. The big news, though, was Bryan Hudson’s clean stat line and very good PFF grade at center. John Michael Schmitz’s absence for his child’s birth opened the door for Hudson to show what he can do, and that will bear watching going forward. A Wally Pipp moment?

PFF grades: Defense

Arvell Reese was nothing short of spectacular on Sunday, grading an amazing 90.5 overall and either very good or elite in all four individual categories (run defense, tackling, pass rush, and pass coverage). This follows on his excellent scores from last week. It’s tempting to say that it’s only taken him a month to adjust to NFL play, but the level of competition has been lower the past two weeks than in the first two weeks. Still, if you want to say that the Giants got the best player in the draft, you probably won’t get many arguments right now. Continuing with the hyperbole, I told Ed that his all-around dominance on Sunday reminded me of the Lawrence Taylor Thanksgiving Day game in Detroit in 1982. Tremaine Edmunds at the other linebacker spot has been less visible, but he did have a sack and eight tackles, despite one missed tackle.

Deonte Banks’ 88.3 yesterday was only the second time PFF has ever graded him above 80. The attention he is getting is for the final two plays of the game, but overall he allowed only three completions in nine targets for 19 yards despite having a ticky-tacky DPI called on him against Marvin Harrison Jr. He did surrender two TDs, but he had the game-saving interception and two other pass breakups (one the play just before the INT). Elsewhere in the secondary, Dru Phillips (76.9), much-maligned as a cover corner, had a crucial breakup of a pass to Michael Wilson in the end zone just before Banks’ two clutch plays to seal the win. Tyler Nubin, Jevon Holland, and Greg Newsome all played adequately.

The defensive line as a unit probably had its best game of the season. D.J. Reader (85.8) made it two games in a row with elite play inside, with a QB hit and a hurry, a tackle and an assist, and no missed tackles. Shelby Harris (70.3) had his best game as a Giant, with three tackles and an assist and a batted pass that led to Reese’s interception. C.J. Okoye (61.6) registered his first NFL sack.

On the edge, Kayvon Thibodeaux’s 59.5 grade reflected his not making the stat sheet except for one assist on a tackle. That was more than made up for by Abdul Carter’s (77.6 overall, 90.1 pass rush) spectacular game rushing the QB, which included three hits and three hurries. That 90.1 led the NFL.

Advanced stats

We saw both sides of the Jameis Winston Experience on Sunday, with three TDs and two INTs (and in PFF’s eyes, four big-time throws and two turnover-worthy throws). That’s what you get with Jameis – no risk it, no biscuit. It’s in his DNA, but it wasn’t all his fault. The Giants’ offensive line did not have a great game yesterday, with 19 pressures (yes, 19), including four sacks and three QB hits. Walter Nolen, Dante Stills, and Josh Sweat were having their way with the Giants IOL yesterday. If you think QB pressure doesn’t matter, here’s the counter-argument:

There’s a lot of scatter, i.e., some QBs still throw well even when pressured (upper right quadrant) and some throw poorly despite not a lot of pressure (lower left). Overall, though, the distribution trends from upper left to lower right, i.e., less/more pressure, fewer/more off-target throws. Jameis had some good company (Patrick Mahomes, Jalen Hurts) in that lower right quadrant.

Considering how much he was pressured, Winston didn’t play that poorly by objective measures such as ESPN’s QBR, which is related to the expected points added concept but with adjustments for the quality of defense faced, and inside or outside garbage time:

Jameis’ aDOT of 11.21 yards was up there with some of the big boys, and his success rate (how much he advanced the offense toward a first down given down and distance to go) was also above average.

The Giants’ running game didn’t give them all that much, however, compared to what we saw at the start of the season (click on the figure to see the bottom rows):

Cam Skattebo was dead last among 28 qualifying running backs. His rush EPA was a poor -3.4 and his success rate an almost as bad 27.8%. John Harbaugh may have envisioned a Giants offense that was going to run the ball down opponents’ throats, but it wasn’t that way against Arizona. There may be several reasons for that: (1) The Giants’ run blocking is below average (7th worst in PFF run block grade) – Andrew Thomas is a very good run blocker but is playing injured; the Giants’ IOLs are as a group below average in run blocking, including rookie Sisi Mauigoa so far; and teams are anticipating the Giants’ run-heavy attack (how could they not after that Dallas opening game) and showing them stacked boxes a lot (33.3% of the time according to the chart in Week 4, 7th highest in the NFL).

The Giants’ receivers were more successful than their running backs yesterday. Here’s a chart of receiving EPA leaders in Week 4:

It’s nice to see Nabers back up there with the league leaders at 10.9 EPA and an even better 1.56 EPA/target (second-best). Say this about Jameis Winston – if he sees you open, he’ll try to hit you. As described by Nick Falato’s podcast partner Dan Schneier:

item.title: NFL Panic Meter: Eagles offense, Lions defense are big problems for 2 marquee NFC teams
item.description: Two of the NFC's marquee teams might already be in trouble.
item.content:encoded:
The two powerhouse teams in the NFC two seasons ago were the 15-2 Detroit Lions, and a Philadelphia Eagles team that went on to win a Super Bowl.

The NFL moves fast. It's only four games into this season but the Eagles and Lions both look incredibly flawed, for different reasons. The Eagles can't move the ball and the Lions can't stop anyone. Both teams can blame injuries, though there are personnel issues too.

The Eagles played most or all of Sunday's game against the Rams without running back Saquon Barkley (hamstring), receiver DeVonta Smith (hamstring), tight end Dallas Goedert and right tackle Lane Johnson (personal reasons). That's arguably the Eagles' three best skill-position players and their best lineman. Without them they gained 172 yards, averaged just 3 yards per play and blew a 10-point lead in the final five minutes. Not great.

Barkley will be week-to-week with his injury and backup Tank Bigsby is going on injured reserve for a core muscle injury. There is no explanation for what's going on with Johnson.

Head coach Nick Sirianni is getting a lot of criticism. Quarterback Jalen Hurts is catching some too; he hasn't played well all season and wasn't great last season either. The offense seems to miss the presence of A.J. Brown, who was traded this offseason. Next up for the Eagles is a tough game at London against the Jaguars. Hurts, who had only 10 yards passing in the second half on Sunday, probably isn't in danger of losing his job if he continues to play poorly. The Eagles just switched backup quarterbacks, demoting Andy Dalton for Tanner McKee. The fact that both have been No. 3 on the depth chart already this season indicates neither one is threatening Hurts no matter how bad he plays. But a productive game would be a reprieve.

There's a way out of the mess for the Eagles, once they start to get healthy. That might not be the case for the Lions.

The Lions have been in prime time twice. Both times a big audience got to see a team that can still move the ball fine but can't get a stop. The Carolina Panthers look much better on offense in Bryce Young's fourth season, but after punting on their first drive here were the Panthers' next six drives: touchdown, touchdown, field goal, touchdown, touchdown, field goal. The Lions are last in the NFL in yards allowed per game and last in points allowed per game. For those who prefer advanced stats, they're last in EPA (expected points added) per play allowed, 29th in success rate allowed and 31st in DVOA. The Lions' offense is top eight in all those stats; that group isn't the problem.

Lions head coach Dan Campbell said he and the Lions knew the Panthers would go to receiver Tetairoa McMillan often with No. 2 receiver Jalen Coker out due to injury. The Lions did nothing to stop him though. He had 14 catches for 192 yards and two touchdowns.

At this point the Lions' defensive issues seem unfixable. A coordinator change can't turn everything around, but Campbell was asked if replacing Kelvin Sheppard was on the table.

"I'm not talking about all that," Campbell said. "I'm talking about getting better right now with what we've got. And that's what we're gonna do. We're going to find a way to get better with what we got."

Cornerback D.J. Reed defended Sheppard, saying after Sunday's game "It's not a coaching thing, it's a players' thing." He might be right, and that brings another set of problems. They're without starting safeties Kerby Joseph and Brian Branch, and also lost defensive back Avonte Maddox to a season-ending injury. Add in the loss of Terrion Arnold, who was cut this offseason after he was arrested, and the Lions secondary is a shell of what it was. At least Branch is "very close" to a return, according to Campbell. Joseph's return doesn't seem imminent. Branch is a good player but even if he returns soon it's not like one safety completely fixes a defense allowing 423.8 yards and 31.8 points per game.

Panic meter: A bad defense seems like it might ruin the Lions season. The same could be true for the Eagles and their offense, though there's some slight hope for a rebound.

Broncos' offensive woes continue

In four games the Broncos have 13 first-half points. That's the second-fewest in the NFL through four games over the last five seasons, according to Josh Dubow of the Associated Press. The 2023 Giants had just nine first-half points through four weeks.

The early problems indicate the script to open the game is not working. That's one of the many problems with the Broncos offense.

Denver has struggled with Sean Payton giving play-calling to offensive coordinator Davis Webb to start the season. Payton has been asked regularly since a terrible Week 1 performance what he thinks of the play-calling, or if he'll take it back. Payton has not given any indication that he will do that. But it will be hard to resist if the offensive problems persist.

"I think the frustrations just come within the losses," quarterback Bo Nix said, according to the Broncos' transcripts. "Obviously, we want to have a really explosive offense and that'll come, but we've played really good teams."

The Broncos have played good teams: Chiefs, Jaguars, Rams and 49ers. That doesn't completely excuse an offense that is 27th in yards per game this season. Something better change soon, or the play-caller will change.

Panic meter: It's early, the Broncos are in decent shape at 2-2, but there are a lot of warning signs.

Lamar Jackson hurt again

The doctors on social media were in overdrive on Sunday, trying to diagnose Jackson's latest injury. Most of them speculated that it was a mild high ankle sprain.

Turns out, he is dealing with an ankle sprain, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, and while Rapoport reported the injury is not "long-term or surgical" — there’s an “outside” chance he could play Sunday night — he could end up missing multiple games.

That's not great for Jackson, and any injury for the Baltimore Ravens quarterback is bad news. We saw how the Ravens' season fell apart last year when Jackson suffered a hamstring injury and wasn't the same when he came back. It appears he will return soon, with an outside chance to play this week, but Baltimore is going to struggle to win any games he misses.

Panic meter: Baltimore hasn't been good when Jackson has missed games, and it's now concerning if the injury will linger even when he returns, which was the case last season.

Will Cardinals make a QB change?

Jacoby Brissett is good enough to run a competent offense. He's also not good enough to make a big difference for the Arizona Cardinals when it comes to winning games.

The Cardinals are 2-14 over the last two seasons when Brissett starts. On Sunday, the Cardinals played a Giants team they could have beaten, but Brissett threw three interceptions, including one on the final play that was returned for a touchdown.

Soon, Brissett will face a series of problems. The Cardinals are realistically going to be out of the playoff race quickly. He hasn't played well enough that the Cardinals would keep starting him despite the losses. He's 33 years old and clearly not the future. The Cardinals have a third-round rookie, Carson Beck, who played well in the Hall of Fame game in the preseason and probably needs a longer look before the end of the season. All of that adds up to a quarterback change sooner rather than later.

Panic meter: Brissett needs to play better quickly, and even that might not be enough.

Rams win, but issues persist

Had Sunday's Rams-Eagles game ended with five minutes left, the conversations this week would have been intense.

The Rams trailed by 10 points and looked to be on the way to a 1-3 start. Matthew Stafford threw two interceptions, giving him six in four games. He had eight all last season. The Rams can't even blame the offensive issues on injuries. They were reasonably healthy. And while the Eagles have a good defense in theory, they were six days removed from being picked apart by Case Keenum, the 38-year-old Bears third-string quarterback.

The Rams saved themselves a week of angst. They scored two late touchdowns to win. They're 2-2, which isn't great, but it's a lot better than 1-3. The Rams get a tough test against the Bills on Monday night in Week 5. Los Angeles avoided a week of grief with a win Sunday, but falling to 2-3 with a loss to the Bills might spark up the discussion about how good the Rams actually are.

Panic meter: The thought that the Rams might just not be great this season is creeping in.

item.title: Ravens' Lamar Jackson reportedly dealing with sprained ankle, has 'outside' chance to play Week 5
item.description: Jackson did not play in the second half of Sunday's win over the Titans.
item.content:encoded:
Baltimore Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson reportedly suffered a sprained ankle during Sunday's 24-18 win over the Tennessee Titans, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

Jackson did not return to the field for the second half and was spotted leaving the locker room in a walking boot. An MRI was scheduled for Monday.

Per Rapoport, there remains an "outside" chance Jackson could play Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons. Depending on how his recovery goes, he is also at risk of missing time. The ankle injury is not considered a long-term ailment or one that would require surgery.

If Jackson cannot go in Week 5, Tyler Huntley, who relieved Jackson against the Titans, would get the start. Huntley went 8-of-9 passing for 63 yards and added 16 rushing yards.

Ravens head coach Jesse Minter told reporters on Monday, "I don't know the chances yet" of Jackson playing in Week 5, and did add, "I don't think it's going to be crazy long-term."

Jackson appeared to sustain the injury on a sack late in the first half by Titans defensive end Jermaine Johnson. The Ravens quarterback was able to stand up from the tackle and walk off the field.

Jermaine with the sack

📺: @NFLonCBSpic.twitter.com/zL6SHLHckO

— Tennessee Titans (@Titans) October 4, 2026

Replays showed that Jackson's left ankle got caughtand twisted under Johnson's body as Johnson sacked him from behind.

Before the injury, Jackson went 15 for 20 for 222 yards and two touchdowns, while adding 20 rushing yards.

Jackson has completed 70.8% of his passes, which, if he sustains that mark, would be a career high. The quarterback has thrown for 967 yards, 6 touchdowns and 1 interception so far. Jackson isn't running as much, but still has an additional 144 yards and another score on the ground.

The Ravens are tied with the Cleveland Browns atop the AFC North through four games. Both teams are 3-1, while the Pittsburgh Steelers and Cincinnati Bengals are 2-2.

item.title: Report: "Outside chance" Lamar Jackson plays in Week 5
item.description: Tyler Huntley would start for the Ravens if Jackson is out.
item.content:encoded:
Signs continue to point toward Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson missing Sunday night's game in Atlanta.

PFT reported that Jackson was considered week-to-week after injuring his ankle in Baltimore's Week 4 win over the Titans with an MRI still to come to determine the extent of the issue. Jackson underwent further evaluation on Monday and Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that there is only an "outside chance" that he will be available against the Falcons.

Jackson's chances of playing in Week 6 will rely on how his sprained ankle responds to treatment.

Tyler Huntley will start for the Ravens as long as Jackson is out of action. Huntley was 8-of-9 for 63 yards in the second half of the win over the Titans and he has started 11 times for Baltimore over the years. He also made five starts for the Dolphins in 2024.

item.title: National NFL All-Rookie Team has 5 Browns, as 2026 NFL Draft class is impressing
item.description: Spencer Fano, KC Concepcion, Denzel Boston lead the way from the Cleveland Browns 2026 NFL Draft class All-Rookie team
item.content:encoded:
When everyone is giving the Cleveland Browns 2026 NFL Draft high grades and words like “a potential home-run class” are being used by a long-time NFL draft analyst, it’s fair to say hopes were high. The 10-person class followed a very good 2025 NFL Draft by GM Andrew Berry and was once again full of top-level athletes.

Many wondered if Berry’s new rookies really could live up to the billing or even the previous draft classes’ performance. Others, like our two different roundtables, were more interested in which of the rookies would have the biggest impact this season.

So far, so great.

On offense, four rookies are starting and playing well: LT Spencer Fano, RG Austin Barber, WR Denzel Boston, and WR KC Concepcion. If you are keeping track, those are four of Cleveland’s top five picks this year. The fifth, S Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, had a breakout game in Week 4.

It is no surprise that those five made Dane Brugler’s (author of the NFL Draft’s “The Beast”) NFL All-Rookie Team through four weeks of the season. The draft expert had a lot of positives to say about the Browns rookies, starting with Boston:

I don’t think there is much debate over the top rookie receivers through four games. And Boston is at the top of the list. The second-rounder leads all rookies with 284 receiving yards, and he and Zay Flowers are the only NFL players with multiple catches of 50-plus yards in 2026.

Boston is one of the best move-the-chain players in the league — 76.9 percent of his catches have resulted in a first down or touchdown, which ranks fifth in the league

Both rookie receivers were first-team selections. As were both offensive linemen:

Before the draft, much was made of Fano’s lack of length, which can show when he attempts to sit down against power (see his NFL debut vs. the Jaguars). But his fluid athleticism allows him to recover and stay out of compromised positions. The Browns’ left tackle played at a high level in Week 4.

The last line of my scouting report on Barber suggested that he “might be better suited for a move to guard.” So far, so good. Barber was a college tackle, but playing inside has helped mask some of his timing issues that showed out in space. His run-blocking tape against the Steelers was outstanding.

The lone defender from Cleveland’s 2026 NFL Draft class to make the list, McNeil-Warren “had a case for the first team” but was honored on the second team by Brugler:

Meanwhile, McNeil-Warren has seen his defensive role grow each week. His pass breakup versus DK Metcalf last Thursday was a thing of beauty, and he has yet to miss a tackle in run support.

Getting five top-level starters out of any draft class is impressive. It will be interesting if the Browns see much production from their five Day 3 rookies this season (C Parker Brailsford, LB Justin Jefferson, TE Joe Royer, QB Taylen Green, TE Carsey Ryan) or if they are mostly developmental players for now.

Through Week 4, only Ryan (2 offensive snaps, 60 on special teams) has played during the regular season.

item.title: Lamar Jackson injury update: Ravens star ‘could miss multiple games’ with ankle sprain
item.description: Lamar Jackson could miss multiple games after spraining his left ankle against the Titans in Week 4.
item.content:encoded:
Update 10/6: Jackson sprained his left ankle against the Titans, and his status for Baltimore’s Week 5 game against the Atlanta Falcons is in jeopardy. NFL insider Ian Rapoport reports that there’s “only an outside chance” Jackson can play against the Falcons. If he can’t go, Tyler Huntley is next up on the depth chart. The good news for the Ravens is that Jackson’s injury isn’t considered serious, according to Rapoport. There’s a chance he could miss multiple games, though. After Atlanta, the Ravens face Cleveland on the road, Cincinnati at home, and Buffalo on the road. Baltimore is in a good spot at 3-1 right now, tied with the Browns atop the AFC North. They need to be careful with Jackson so they don’t risk aggravating the injury later in the season.

Here’s the full report from Rapoport.

Postgame update: Jackson did not return as the Ravens went on to beat the Titans, 24-18. Jackson left the stadium in a protective boot. Head coach Jessie Minter updated Jackson’s condition after the game, saying “we don’t know enough about it right now” when asked how Jackson’s ankle is feeling. Minter said there was discussion about putting Jackson back in the game, but he stayed on the bench while Baltimore did just enough to win. Jackson is believed to be day-to-day, according to insider Ian Rapoport.

Lamar Jackson is questionable to return after spraining his ankle against the Tennessee Titans in Week 4. Jackson was tripped up by a Titans defender during the third quarter and hurt his ankle on the play. He was replaced by Tyler Huntley at QB.

Watch the play here:

Jackson was on the sidelines for the Ravens’ next drive:

Baltimore was already up 24-7 at the time of the injury. Jackson is 15-of-20 for 222 yards, two touchdowns, and no interceptions through the air so far.

The Ravens are in full control against Tennessee, and probably won’t even need Jackson to finish off this win. The Titans entered the week as one of four winless teams throughout the NFL this season.

We’ll update this story as it develops.

item.title: Can’t blame the flags for Bills loss to New England Patriots
item.description: Despite the eye test, flags were the least of Buffalo Bills worries in humiliating loss to Patriots
item.content:encoded:
Well that game sucked. Like… really, really sucked. But it wasn’t because of the penalties! I know a couple seemed like a big deal at the time, but in the grand scheme of things, the flags the Buffalo Bills were called for had very little impact on the outcome of the game. I also don’t think the refs were perfect in this one, but the mistakes weren’t all that meaningful. The good news is that this recap should be way less aggravating than the actual game was.

Standard and Advanced Metrics

Penalty Counts

Now, I knew that they didn’t have a high count like last week but I was actually a bit shocked to see only five flags were assessed on the Bills. Two were declined so seven were called in total but that’s five less than against the Chargers. Remember my philosophy on declined flags too. It’s not great it was called but something worse for your team happened on the snap so it’s not like the penalty hurt ya at all.

Penalty Yards

This was just as surprising to me. There was basically no yardage lost with both teams coming in way under average. Now if you take a look at official box scores, the Bills had 31 assessed yards. The difference is that a kick failing to reach the landing zone isn’t “assessed” any yards officially, the ball just “magically” starts at the 40 rather than the 35. I take the five yards and call it assessed. It doesn’t sit right with me that an enforced penalty that changes the spot of the ball gets recorded as a zero.

For the segue into the advanced metrics, a quick way to jack up the Harm rating is to have a bunch of impacted yards. The chart to the right is the first indicator that the Harm isn’t going to be very high. Neither team impacted/negated much yardage.

Penalty Harm

New England Patriots

The total Harm for the Patriots was 9.3, which approached our bad day threshold of 10.0 Harm, and is close enough to say there was some impact from flags. A large part of this was due to the offensive holding flag on Will Campbell. On 3rd & 7, Drake Maye scrambled for 10 yards to pick up the first. The flag negated those ten yards, was assessed for the usual ten, and negated two downs. The Patriots ended up punting as a result.

Marcus Jones’ defensive holding flag was similar. On 3rd & 16 the Bills dialed up an incomplete pass. In field goal range and only down by seven early on, it’s likely that Buffalo takes the field goal. Instead, the drive continues and Buffalo scores a touchdown. That touchdown was also made five yards easier thanks to a half-the-distance-to-the-goal flag courtesy of Mike Vrabel’s attitude.

The Patriots won, Vrabel called a good game, and they deserve that credit; but holy heck was that one of the most cringe, whiny, take my ball and go home temper tantrums I’ve seen in a long while.

Buffalo Bills

I said that the refs didn’t impact the outcome much for the Bills so let’s get right to it. They had a grand total of 5.9 Harm, which is the lowest single game total by anyone so far this season (second lowest was 7.6 by the Chargers).

The face mask by Sam Franklin was yards only and on a deep punt so it wasn’t ideal but only impacted starting field position. Most of the flags were yardage only like this one. Connor McGovern’s offensive offside negated a one yard gain.

The biggest story was Max Hairston’s defensive holding call. The flag itself was only one yard, but wiped out a two yard sack. It also gave up two free downs. It’s possible that Vrabel goes for it, already showing he planned on a being aggressive. It’s possible that Buffalo can make a stop on 4th & 4. It’s also possible it’s a field goal. Maybe there’s zero change in the outcome of the drive, but maybe this flag was worth four or seven points to the Patriots.

In a three point game. Let’s take a look now and see what we can learn from these flags.

  • I really wanted to take a look at McGovern’s offside call. Offensive offsides is not at all common with only one or two a week all season. Put differently, if you’re not watching the right game, you could go weeks without seeing one. I wanted to see if McGovern moved the ball from where the official spotted it. He did not. I wanted to see if he was leaning over the ball too far. He was not. Finally, I wanted to see if any part of him was past the ball. There was not. I don’t see any reason this was called.
  • On Bass’ kickoff short of the landing zone, going frame by frame it looks like the ball was juuuuuust shy of the landing zone. What’s wild to me is that (watch the video if you haven’t yet) the official that calls it is nowhere near the line itself and somehow saw this. He’s close to 30 yards away when it hits and not staring down the line. Wild!
  • The Dawkins hold is mostly legit, but I’m going to invoke a rule that only I ever seem to bring up. The defender’s right arm swings almost like he’s trying a rip move. Remember that if a defender tries a rip holding isn’t supposed to be called unless his “feet are taken away from him” which is not the case here. I want to be clear here that I don’t think the defender is trying a rip move and this is a good call. However, I have the luxury of focusing on just Dawkins and replay at my leisure. The official has to call this in real time with one shot and it’d be understandable in this case if he thought there was a rip and it wasn’t called.
  • The illegal hands to the face by Dawkins was clearly the right call.
  • Davison Igbinosun definitely seems to impact his man’s movement and ability to make a catch and this was a good call too. It could have been worse though seeing as how Mack Hollins still made the catch.
  • On the Max Hairston flag, I don’t love this one at all. Technically I think you can call this, but how many times have you seen an undershirt pull not get called because the receiver can run free uninhibited? I don’t see any restriction on the ability to make a catch which isn’t technically part of defensive holding’s definition/guidance in the rulebook but in practicality we see it play out that way.
  • Finally, Sam Franklin had a heck of a face mask. 100% the right call.

item.title: Ravens QB Lamar Jackson injury updates could impact Browns Week 6 chances
item.description: The Cleveland Browns schedule could get much easier if Ravens QB Lamar Jackson misses Week 6 with an injury
item.content:encoded:
When it comes to looking ahead to the next quarter of the Cleveland Browns schedule, the Baltimore Ravens in Week 6 look to be the toughest of the four matchups. As we all know, injuries continue to be the biggest storyline across the NFL. The Browns are dealing with DT Mason Graham being out for a few weeks, while the Los Angeles Rams (important because of the big trade between the two teams) have been without a few star players, including DE Myles Garrett, but have steadied the ship at 2-2.

If Cleveland is able to continue their surprising start to the season, the team will need some good injury luck. Whether that is fewer injuries for them or more injuries for their opponents, fans will want to keep an eye on the weekly injury reports.

While the Browns will have to get ready for the New York Jets in Week 5, the Ravens matchup in Week 6 is on the horizon, and the AFC North co-leader is dealing with an injury to QB Lamar Jackson, who left Week 4 in a walking boot due to an ankle injury.

An update from Baltimore HC Jesse Minter indicated that there was a chance that Jackson could play in Week 5, but the Ravens quarterback has been cautious in his return timing most of his career. Minter’s language was vague:

Former Browns QB Tyler Huntley would likely take the snaps for the Ravens, with their former offensive coordinator now Cleveland’s head coach, Todd Monken.

In an update, it seems like Jackson’s injury could linger into Week 6, but that Baltimore has no reason to tip their hands, even for Week 5:

We will keep tracking Jackson’s injury status on the way toward the Browns versus Ravens in Week 6.

Do you think Jackson plays versus the Browns in 2 weeks? If not, how does that change your expectations?
